Some are citizens of the United States, Canada and Australia, and some were never residents of Hong Kong at all. They live in Britain, America, Canada, Australia and Taiwan, and most of them are doing in exile what they did at home: speaking, writing, testifying and organising. Since **July 2023**, Hong Kong's national security police have issued arrest warrants, with cash rewards attached, for **34 people living abroad**. The Hong Kong government alleges secession, subversion and collusion with foreign forces, but almost every allegation it has published describes things they said, lobbied for, testified about or voted in. **None of them has been arrested, and no reward has been reported paid.** Because the government cannot reach them, the pressure falls on the people it can reach: **their parents, siblings and cousins in Hong Kong**. This page is a record of the people and of what has been done to them. It is **not a wanted list**. It reprints no police notices, and it gives countries rather than locations. > *"I am just a Hong Konger speaking out for Hong Kongers – that's all."* — **Nathan Law**, after the first warrants in 2023 ([CNN via KRDO](https://krdo.com/?p=992212)) ## The people | 他們是誰
Freely licensed photographs exist for only some of the people named. Christopher Mung, Carmen Lau, Tony Chung, Chloe Cheung, Victor Ho, Joe Tay, Johnny Fok, Tony Choi and the fifteen people named in 2025 have none we can use. Every portrait above shows its subject in public life: speaking, testifying, campaigning. Several were taken before their subjects left Hong Kong. ### Lawmakers and lawyers **Nathan Law 羅冠聰** led students in the 2014 Umbrella Movement and co-founded Demosistō. In 2016, at 23, he became the youngest person ever elected to the Legislative Council, and he was disqualified over his oath a year later. He left Hong Kong on 2 July 2020, the day after the National Security Law took effect, and was granted asylum in Britain in 2021. He has since testified to the US Congress and written two books, *Freedom: How We Lose It and How We Fight Back* (2021) and *When the Wind Blows* (2024) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Law)). After the warrant he warned: *"There will be people who are incentivized to give out my information, my whereabouts"* ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/china-hong-kong-democracy-activists-dissidents-bounty-nathan-law-rcna92512)). **Dennis Kwok 郭榮鏗** is a barrister and a founding member of the Civic Party. He represented the legal profession in LegCo from 2012 until Beijing's disqualification of four legislators in November 2020, which led fifteen pro-democracy colleagues to resign in protest. In the US he has held scholarly posts at Georgetown and Harvard's Kennedy School. Both the New York City Bar and the New York State Bar condemned the warrant against him ([NYC Bar](https://www.nycbar.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Hong_Kong_Bounties.pdf); [NYSBA](https://nysba.org/?p=143552)). **Ted Hui 許智峯** is a solicitor. He was a district councillor from 2012 and a Democratic Party legislator for Hong Kong Island from 2016 to 2020. He left in December 2020 while on bail over a 2019 protest, and was admitted as a solicitor in Australia, which granted him and his family protection visas in August 2025 ([ABC](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-08-17/ted-hui-granted-asylum-protection-in-australia/105664062)). His answer to the bounty: *"I will continue to live an ordinary, normal life"* ([SBS](https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/why-has-hong-kong-put-a-bounty-on-these-activists-in-australia/1sa7o4c7c)). **Kevin Yam 任建峰**, an Australian citizen, practised financial-regulatory and litigation law in Hong Kong for more than 17 years and co-founded the Progressive Lawyers Group in 2015. He is now a senior fellow at Georgetown Law's Center for Asian Law ([Lawfare](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/contributors/kyam)). *"It's my duty ... to continue to speak out against the crackdown that is going on right now,"* he said ([SBS](https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/why-has-hong-kong-put-a-bounty-on-these-activists-in-australia/1sa7o4c7c)). When letters offering the reward reached his neighbours in 2025, he said: *"I will continue to live my everyday life. … I will not voluntarily return to Hong Kong before it is free."* ([ABC](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-03-18/melbourne-residents-receive-letter-offering-money-kevin-yam/105065392)). **Carmen Lau 劉珈汶** won a district council seat in 2019 and resigned in 2021 rather than take the new loyalty oath, refusing to be a "pawn of tyranny". In Britain she works with the Hong Kong Democracy Council on political prisoners ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2024/12/28/explainer-who-are-the-six-overseas-activists-facing-new-hong-kong-nat-security-arrest-warrants/)), and in 2026 she testified at the UN Human Rights Council ([ISHR](https://ishr.ch/latest-updates/hrc63-hong-kong-defenders-highlight-transnational-repression-as-states-renew-concerns-over-china/)). *"The bounty is because they want to silence us and they want to instill fear among our diaspora. … I will just continue my work because if I back down or if I really silence myself, that's what they want."* ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/uk-bounty-hong-kong-democracy-activist-china-rcna194068)). ### A unionist and a pollster **Christopher Mung 蒙兆達** spent decades in the labour movement and helped lead the Hong Kong Confederation of Trade Unions before it was forced to disband in 2021. In Britain he founded **Hong Kong Labour Rights Monitor**. Unions in six countries and the International Trade Union Confederation asked for the warrant against him to be withdrawn ([HKLRM](https://hklabourrights.org/newsletter/july-2023/)). When his passport was cancelled in 2024 he said: *"You can cancel my passport, but you can never cancel my identity as a Hong Kong citizen."* ([VOA](https://www.voanews.com/a/hong-kong-cancels-passports-of-six-self-exiled-democracy-activists/7654211.html)). **Chung Kim-wah 鍾劍華** is a former social worker and social-policy scholar whose research backed universal pensions and standard working hours. He was deputy chief executive of the Hong Kong Public Opinion Research Institute, and left for Britain in 2022 after police scrutiny of its polling, saying Hong Kong had become a place where one could "no longer live normally and without intimidation" ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2024/12/28/explainer-who-are-the-six-overseas-activists-facing-new-hong-kong-nat-security-arrest-warrants/)). He writes political commentary from exile. ### Young organisers and advocates **Finn Lau 劉祖廸**, a surveyor, wrote anonymously in 2019 as "I want Lam Chau" (我要攬炒), proposing that Hongkongers lobby foreign governments to sanction officials. He founded Hong Kong Liberty and has lived in London since 2020 ([HKFP, 2020](https://hongkongfp.com/2020/10/25/wanted-hong-kong-activist-finn-lau-behind-the-faceless-laam-caau-persona-says-he-will-seize-any-chance-of-survival-and-give-back/)). *"This sort of bounty or safety risks will not deter me from continuing advocating for Hong Kong human rights and democracy."* ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/china-hong-kong-democracy-activists-dissidents-bounty-nathan-law-rcna92512)). **Anna Kwok 郭鳳儀** ran crowd-funded international campaigns during the 2019 protests under an online alias. She is now executive director of the Washington-based **Hong Kong Democracy Council**, and has testified to the US Congressional-Executive Commission on China in 2023 and 2026 ([CECC](https://www.cecc.gov/sites/evo-subsites/cecc.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/anna-kwok_testimony.pdf)). Her father became the first relative of a wanted activist to be jailed (see below). **Simon Cheng 鄭文傑** worked on trade and investment at the British Consulate-General in Hong Kong. In August 2019 he was detained in mainland China, where he says he was shackled, hooded, deprived of sleep and made to record confessions. Britain granted him asylum in 2020, and he founded **Hongkongers in Britain** to help new arrivals settle ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Cheng)). His response to the bounty: *"Being hunted by China (Hong Kong)'s secret police, under a one-million-dollar bounty, is a lifelong honor"* ([Reuters via Himalayan Times](https://thehimalayantimes.com/world/hong-kong-offers-awards-for-arrests-of-activists-abroad-for-breaching-national-security-law)). **Frances Hui 許穎婷** joined the student group Scholarism as a teenager. As a journalism student in Boston she wrote the 2019 column "I am from Hong Kong, Not China". In 2022 she was reportedly the first Hongkonger granted asylum by the US federal government ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_Hui)). She leads **We The Hongkongers** and has said her advocacy will not stop. **Joey Siu 邵嵐** was born in the US and grew up in Hong Kong. She was a university student-union leader in 2019, and in 2023 became the first US citizen made a fugitive under the National Security Law. She has testified to two US Senate committees ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Siu)). *"My response to the Chinese Communist regime's intimidation is short: I will never be silenced, I will never back down."* ([Nikkei Asia](https://asia.nikkei.com/Editor-s-Picks/Interview/Hong-Kong-activist-Joey-Siu-describes-transnational-repression-by-China)). **Tony Chung 鍾翰林** led the student group Studentlocalism. Arrested outside the US Consulate in 2020, he was jailed for 3 years 7 months, at the time the youngest person imprisoned under the National Security Law. After his release under supervision he described "deep surveillance and immense pressure", and offers of money to inform on fellow activists. He left at the end of 2023 and was granted refugee status in Britain in 2025. *"I already miss Hong Kong. It was a very difficult decision to make."* ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/dec/29/i-already-miss-hong-kong-democracy-activist-tony-chung-on-fleeing-to-the-uk)). **Chloe Cheung 張晞晴** moved to Britain in 2020, aged 15. At 19 she became the youngest person ever targeted, and in 2025 she gave evidence on transnational repression to Parliament's Joint Committee on Human Rights ([CFHK](https://thecfhk.org/cfhk-foundations-chloe-cheung-testifies-to-uk-parliament-on-transnational-repression/)). *"How fragile, incompetent, and cowardly does a regime have to be to believe that I, a 19-year-old, ordinary Hongkonger, can 'endanger' and 'divide' the country? … Even in the face of a powerful enemy, I will continue to do what I believe is right."* ([CBC/AP](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/hong-kong-arrest-warrants-bounties-activists-1.7418476)). ### Journalists and commentators **Victor Ho 何良懋**, a Canadian citizen, is a former editor-in-chief of the Vancouver edition of *Sing Tao Daily*. He told CBC he would not be deterred ([CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/hong-kong-rewards-exiles-canada-1.7594040)). **Joe Tay 鄭敬基**, also a Canadian citizen, is a former singer and TVB/RTHK actor who co-founded the YouTube channel **HongKonger Station**. In 2025 he stood as a federal Conservative candidate. Canada's election-security task force identified an online repression campaign against him during the race ([CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/joe-tay-china-campaign-1.7514934)). **Elmer Yuen 袁弓夷** is a businessman and online commentator who lobbied Washington for sanctions in 2019–20. He co-founded the effort that became the overseas "Hong Kong Parliament", and of the 2025 warrant he remarked: *"It helps us with a lot of advertising"* ([CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/hong-kong-rewards-exiles-canada-1.7594040)). **Johnny Fok 霍嘉誌** and **Tony Choi 蔡明達** co-founded the current-affairs YouTube channel 「升旗易得道」. ### The diaspora vote In May 2025, Hongkongers abroad held an unofficial online election for a "Hong Kong Parliament", casting about **15,700 valid votes** ([CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/hong-kong-rewards-exiles-canada-1.7594040)). Two months later police issued warrants for its organisers and elected members, and in December 2025 the group was banned. Membership or support in Hong Kong now carries up to 14 years ([info.gov.hk](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202512/02/P2025120200269.htm)). The fifteen people newly named were: - Organisers: **Chan Lai-chun 陳麗珍**, **Feng Chongyi 馮崇義**, **Sasha Gong 龔小夏**, **Ng Man-yan 吳文昕** and **Tsang Wai-fan 曾偉藩**. - Elected members: **Chin Po-fun 錢寶芬**, **Paul Ha 夏海俊**, **Hau Chung-yu 侯中宇**, **Colin Ho 何永友**, **Alan Keung 姜嘉偉**, **Tony Lam 林千淦**, **Agnes Ng 吳文君**, **Wong Chun-wah 黃振華**, **Wong Sau-wo 黃修和** and **Zhang Xinyan 張信燕**. Several have no connection to Hong Kong residence at all: - **Feng Chongyi** is an Australian China-studies scholar who was once detained in China himself ([Chinese PEN](https://www.chinesepen.org/english/uts-professor-chongyi-feng-detained-in-china-stopped-from-boarding-return-flight-to-australia)). - **Sasha Gong**, a US citizen, once directed Voice of America's China Branch. She says she is "not a Hong Kong resident" ([CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/hong-kong-rewards-exiles-canada-1.7594040)). - **Zhang Xinyan** is a mainland Chinese dissident and UN-recognised refugee. She was detained in Thailand in 2026 and blocked from a resettlement flight, then reached Canada in August 2026 after pressure from Ottawa and the UN refugee agency ([HRW](https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/07/14/thailand-dont-forcibly-return-chinese-dissidents); [CP24/AFP](https://cp24.com/news/canada/2026/08/07/chinese-activist-held-in-bangkok-finds-canada-refuge)). **Chin Po-fun**, a retired correctional-services officer, had her government pension stopped ([The Collective HK](https://thecollectivehk.com/%E9%A6%99%E6%B8%AF%E8%AD%B0%E6%9C%83%E6%A1%88%E9%8C%A2%E5%AF%B6%E8%8A%AC%E9%81%AD%E5%87%8D%E7%B5%90%E6%88%B6%E5%8F%A3%E5%81%9C%E9%80%80%E4%BC%91%E9%87%91%E6%94%BF%E5%BA%9C%E7%99%BC%E8%A8%80%E4%BA%BA/)). Several of the fifteen have almost no public record. That is part of the point: this round reached ordinary participants in an overseas vote, not just well-known figures. *Not in the count:* **Agnes Chow 周庭**, Demosistō co-founder and former political prisoner, left for Canada and did not report on bail at the end of 2023. Police declared her wanted in February 2024 and said she "will be pursued for life", but announced no reward ([SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-and-crime/article/3251172/hong-kong-opposition-activist-agnes-chow-declared-wanted-police-jumping-bail-after-fleeing-canada)). ## What has been done to their families | 家人的代價 The exiles are out of reach, so the measures that bite are aimed at the people around them. Human Rights Watch says authorities "have sought to intimidate dozens of their family members, primarily by interrogating them", which it calls "collective punishment, prohibited by international human rights law" ([HRW, May 2025](https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/05/04/hong-kong-targeting-exiled-activists-families-escalates)). The Hong Kong Democracy Council counted **38 relatives and 12 associates** taken in for questioning by the end of 2024 ([EU annual report](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-13533-2026-INIT/en/pdf)). **A father jailed.** In April 2025 police arrested **Kwok Yin-sang**, Anna Kwok's father, and her brother. Her brother was released without charge. Her father was charged with trying to deal with an "absconder's" funds: he had tried to cancel an insurance policy he bought for his daughter when she was two, worth about **HK$88,609**. *"I paid for the policy. She is no longer in Hong Kong, so I canceled it,"* he told police ([The Standard](https://www.thestandard.com.hk/news/article/324227/Father-of-wanted-fugitive-Anna-Kwok-found-guilty-of-handling-absconders-assets)). He was convicted in February 2026 and jailed for **eight months**, the first person convicted of this offence. The magistrate said: "There is no such thing as … collective punishment" ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/2026/02/26/nx-s1-5727437/father-activist-sentenced-hong-kong)). His daughter called it *"guilt by blood, this is hostage taking. This is transnational repression."* Before the sentencing she told Reuters: *"Asian dads are not very known for showing affection with hugs and I realized this year, I actually … don't think I've ever hugged my dad since I became an adult"* ([Reuters via WDEZ](https://wdez.com/?p=914130)). **Relatives questioned.** Parents, siblings, in-laws and cousins of at least sixteen of the people named have been taken in for questioning since 2023. They include the families of Nathan Law, Dennis Kwok, Christopher Mung, Ted Hui, Frances Hui, Simon Cheng, Chung Kim-wah, Carmen Lau, Tony Chung and Joe Tay, and in 2025 the families of four "Hong Kong Parliament" members ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2024/01/11/hong-kong-national-security-police-question-simon-chengs-family-as-exiled-activist-gives-blessing-to-sever-ties/); [RFA](https://rfa.org/english/china/2025/01/23/china-hong-kong-police-question-exiled-pollster-family/); [HRW](https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/05/04/hong-kong-targeting-exiled-activists-families-escalates)). The summonses tend to follow new warrants or bursts of advocacy abroad. Cutting ties publicly has not protected anyone. Simon Cheng told his parents: *"If needed, criticise me and cut me off… My hope is that my parents can enjoy a dignified, peaceful, and serene old age."* ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2024/01/11/hong-kong-national-security-police-question-simon-chengs-family-as-exiled-activist-gives-blessing-to-sever-ties/)). Chung Kim-wah asked: *"My brothers and sisters are all adults, so why should they be held responsible for what I do?"* ([RFA](https://rfa.org/english/china/2025/01/23/china-hong-kong-police-question-exiled-pollster-family/)). **Neighbours, inboxes and spies abroad.** - **Letters to neighbours.** In early 2025, letters copying the police notices reached the neighbours of Carmen Lau and Tony Chung in Britain, and of Kevin Yam in Australia, inviting them to deliver the activist to the Chinese embassy ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/world/uk-bounty-hong-kong-democracy-activist-china-rcna194068); [ABC](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-03-18/melbourne-residents-receive-letter-offering-money-kevin-yam/105065392)). The Hong Kong government said it "would not issue anonymous letters"; no sender has been identified. - **Sexualised fakes.** Later in 2025 the attacks turned sexual: a sexualised poster targeting one activist's wife, and digitally altered explicit images of Carmen Lau sent to her former neighbours. *"Sexualised disinformation has long been used to silence women who challenge authoritarian power,"* Lau said ([Reuters via MarketScreener](https://uk.marketscreener.com/news/exiled-hong-kong-democracy-activists-say-they-re-targeted-by-fake-sexualised-images-ce7d50dbdf8ff32c)). - **A Canadian MP's remark.** In Canada a sitting MP suggested people could take Joe Tay to the Chinese consulate to claim the reward. He withdrew as a candidate after the RCMP said it was looking into the remark ([RCI](https://ici.radio-canada.ca/rci/en/news/2152380/liberal-candidate-paul-chiang-withdraws-from-race-after-suggesting-people-claim-chinas-bounty-on-conservative)). - **Spying in Britain.** In May 2026 a London jury convicted the office manager of the **Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office** and a former UK Border Force officer of assisting a foreign intelligence service by researching UK-based dissidents. They were jailed for 8 and 10 years ([CPS](https://www.cps.gov.uk/cps/news/updated-sentence-cps-secures-convictions-hong-kong-unlawful-surveillance-case)). **The wider community.** In a 2026 survey of more than 1,000 Hongkongers in Britain, **86%** said that joining public events there puts their families in Hong Kong at risk ([Hong Kong Watch](https://www.hongkongwatch.org/all-posts/2026/5/11/new-hong-kong-watch-survey-research-on-tnr-calls-for-enhanced-foreign-interference-measures)). The pressure built for 34 people reaches hundreds of thousands. ## The record | 紀錄 Each round paired court warrants with police reward notices, and every reward has been renewed rather than allowed to lapse. The Hong Kong Police's own list, checked on **20 October 2026**, still shows exactly **34 cases, with no name added since July 2025** ([police.gov.hk](https://www.police.gov.hk/info/appeals_public/nsc/en.xml)). Names below use the official Chinese forms. Several are widely misspelled elsewhere; 霍嘉誌, 劉珈汶, 張晞晴 and 陳麗珍 are correct. | Date | People newly named | Reward announced | Running total | |---|---|---|---| | **3 Jul 2023** ([info.gov.hk](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202307/03/P2023070300526.htm)) | Nathan Law 羅冠聰, Dennis Kwok 郭榮鏗, Ted Hui 許智峯, Kevin Yam 任建峰, Elmer Yuen 袁弓夷, Christopher Mung 蒙兆達, Finn Lau 劉祖廸, Anna Kwok 郭鳳儀 | HK$1 million each | 8 | | **14 Dec 2023** ([info.gov.hk](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202312/14/P2023121400617.htm)) | Simon Cheng 鄭文傑, Frances Hui 許穎婷, Joey Siu 邵嵐, Johnny Fok 霍嘉誌, Tony Choi 蔡明達 | HK$1 million each | 13 | | **24 Dec 2024** ([info.gov.hk](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202412/24/P2024122400514.htm)) | Carmen Lau 劉珈汶, Tony Chung 鍾翰林, Chung Kim-wah 鍾劍華, Chloe Cheung 張晞晴, Victor Ho 何良懋, Joe Tay 鄭敬基 | HK$1 million each | 19 | | **25 Jul 2025** ([info.gov.hk](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202507/25/P2025072500736.htm)) | Fifteen organisers and members of the "Hong Kong Parliament" (above); four people already named were also re-charged | HK$200,000 each | **34** | When the first eight were named, Chief Executive John Lee said: *"The only way to end their destiny of being an abscondee who will be pursued for life is to surrender."* ([info.gov.hk transcript](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202307/04/P2023070400316.htm)). ## How the law reaches abroad | 法律如何越境 - **The claim to reach anyone, anywhere.** Article 38 of the 2020 National Security Law applies it to offences "committed against the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region from outside the Region by a person who is not a permanent resident of the Region". Article 37 covers permanent residents abroad. Officials call this "protective jurisdiction". The UN Human Rights Committee faulted its "lack of clarity" in 2022 and called for the law's repeal ([UN CCPR](https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/4002782/files/CCPR_C_CHN-HKG_CO_4-EN.pdf)). - **The "absconder" regime.** Under the **Safeguarding National Security Ordinance** (in force 23 March 2024), the Security Secretary can declare a wanted person abroad a "specified absconder". That cancels their Hong Kong passport, suspends professional qualifications and removes them from company boards. It also makes it a crime, punishable by up to **seven years**, for anyone in Hong Kong to give them money, deal with their money, rent them property or go into business with them. **29 of the 34** have been specified, in three rounds: 12 June 2024, 24 December 2024 and 4 August 2025 ([info.gov.hk](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202508/04/P2025080400303.htm)). We have found no appeal route in the text. - **Assets.** In February 2025 a court granted an order confiscating Ted Hui's assets without a trial, under rules that require only that he "could have been convicted" ([info.gov.hk](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202502/18/P2025021800005.htm)). - **But no way to bring anyone back.** The UK, US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Germany and France all suspended extradition with Hong Kong in 2020. Interpol's constitution bars it from political cases. Hong Kong officials have conceded they cannot arrest the exiles unless they return. Jurisdiction without enforcement is why the weight falls on families, documents and money still inside Hong Kong. ## How the world has responded | 國際回應 - **Every round has been condemned.** Britain, the United States, Australia, Canada and the EU have issued statements, each most forcefully once its own citizens or residents were named. In August 2025 the **G7** jointly called the practice "transnational repression" that "undermines national security, state sovereignty, human rights, and the safety of communities" ([GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/g7-rapid-response-mechanism-rrm-statement-on-hong-kong-arrest-warrants)). - **Only Washington has sanctioned anyone.** In March 2025 the US sanctioned six Hong Kong officials, including the Secretary for Justice and the Police Commissioner, citing the targeting of "19 pro-democracy activists… including a U.S. citizen and four other U.S. residents" ([State Department](https://www.state.gov/u-s-sanctions-six-individuals-for-undermining-hong-kongs-autonomy)). As one British MP told the Commons in March 2026, *"the UK, which used to run Hong Kong, has sanctioned absolutely nobody"* ([Hansard](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2026-03-03/debates/C629FE3B-7C63-4C81-B7E2-4C5A4BA98BEF)). - **Protection.** Britain, Australia and Canada have granted asylum, refugee status or resettlement to several of those named. Britain also convicted the Hong Kong trade office's London manager and a Border Force officer of spying on dissidents, and Canada's foreign-influence registry took effect in August 2026. - **Hong Kong's answer** to every statement has been the same: extraterritoriality "is in fact a common feature of national security laws", and "No country should harbour criminals" ([info.gov.hk](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202307/04/P2023070400443.htm)). ## What comes next | 接下來 - **November 2026: Interpol's General Assembly meets in Hong Kong.** Advocates are pressing Interpol to confirm that Red Notices will not be used against recognised victims of transnational repression. They note it "is offering no assurance that it has not received Red Notice requests against these activists since the bounties were imposed in 2023" ([Hong Kong Watch](https://www.hongkongwatch.org/all-posts/2026/7/8/hong-kong-watch-patrons-in-uk-and-canada-demand-transparency-from-interpol-ahead-of-its-general-assembly-in-hong-kong)). - **11 and 23 December 2026:** the rewards from the December 2023 and December 2024 rounds expire. Every reward so far has been renewed. - **The likely direction:** fewer new names, and more pressure on the people around them. The 2025 group ban and the conviction of Anna Kwok's father give police new routes to prosecute supporters and relatives inside Hong Kong. We will update this page as events unfold. ## Help complete this record This record is incomplete. Most of the people named in 2025 have almost no public profile, and much of what happens to families is never reported. If you can contribute a freely licensed photograph, a correction, or testimony (yours, or that of someone who has asked for it to be recorded), please see **[[Participation|participation]]**. Related: [[✊ Faces of the Crackdown|faces-of-the-crackdown]] | [[⚖️ Jimmy Lai|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]] | [[📕 Book Censorship under the NSL|book-censorship]] | [[🕯️ Tiananmen Vigil|tiananmen-vigil]]

For a generation Hong Kong had one of the **freest presses in Asia** — a noisy, competitive media market protected by the Basic Law's guarantee of press freedom, where Reporters Without Borders once ranked the city **18th in the world** (2002). In the space of five years that was dismantled. The two biggest independent newsrooms were **raided and shut**, their editors jailed; a **colonial-era sedition law** was revived and then sharpened into a weapon carrying years in prison; and by 2025 RSF had dropped Hong Kong to **140th of 180**, into the "**red zone**" of "very serious" repression for the first time, placing it alongside mainland China. This page gathers that record — the outlets destroyed, the journalists prosecuted, and the laws used to do it — and links to the newsrooms this archive has preserved.

> Since 2020 the Hong Kong government has prosecuted **at least 28 journalists**, eight of whom were in custody as of 2025 (Reporters Without Borders). *"At RSF, we have never seen such a sharp and rapid deterioration in the press-freedom record of any country or territory."*

## A free press, dismantled year by year

| Year | What happened |
|------|---------------|
| **2020** | The **National Security Law** takes effect (30 June). On **10 Aug**, 200 police raid the **Apple Daily** newsroom and arrest founder **Jimmy Lai** under the NSL. |
| **2021** | **Apple Daily** is destroyed: a second raid (**17 June**) arrests five executives and freezes the company's assets; starved of funds, the paper prints its **last edition on 24 June** — **1 million copies**. **RTHK**, the public broadcaster, is brought to heel under a new civil-servant director: programmes are deleted and archives pulled. On **29 Dec**, police raid **Stand News**, arresting senior staff; the outlet closes the same day. |
| **2022** | **Citizen News**, citing the "sword" hanging over the industry, closes pre-emptively on **4 Jan**. The **FCC** suspends its Human Rights Press Awards rather than risk breaking the law. Independent outlets shut or go quiet across the board. |
| **2024** | Hong Kong's homegrown **Article 23** law — the **Safeguarding National Security Ordinance** (23 Mar) — raises the penalty for **sedition** from 2 years to **7** (10 with an "external force"). In the first journalist sedition convictions since 1997, two **Stand News** editors are jailed (see below). **RFA** closes its Hong Kong bureau, citing the new law. |
| **2025** | RSF's World Press Freedom Index puts Hong Kong at **140/180**, its lowest ever score, in the "**red zone**" for the first time. |
| **2026** | Prosecutions reach **independent online media**: an outlet operator (**Boom News**) and an activist are arrested for "**seditious acts**" over filming a public commemoration — released on bail, no charge laid, then the operator's **personal bank accounts are frozen** (7 Oct) with no formal order shown (see below). Separately, ordinary Hongkongers are jailed for **Facebook posts**: a retiree is given a year for 53 seditious posts attacking the authorities — among them comments tying the [[Wang Fuk Court fire|hong-kong-fire-2025]] to possible 2019-style unrest. |

## The two newsrooms that were destroyed

### Apple Daily (蘋果日報)

The city's largest pro-democracy tabloid, founded by **Jimmy Lai** in 1995. Raided under the National Security Law in August 2020 and again in June 2021, when its assets were frozen and five senior executives arrested; unable to pay staff or suppliers, it published its **final edition on 24 June 2021**, a million copies snapped up across the city. Lai and several editors remain on trial or convicted in the long-running NSL case. The paper's full run is preserved here: [[Apple Daily|sites.appledaily]] and its [[publications & special editions|sites.appledaily.publications]]; Lai's own story is on the [[Jimmy Lai|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]] page.

### Stand News (立場新聞)

The flagship of Hong Kong's post-*Apple* independent media, raided and closed on **29 December 2021**. In the first use of the colonial sedition offence against journalists since the 1997 handover, chief editor **Chung Pui-kuen** and acting chief editor **Patrick Lam** were **convicted on 29 August 2024** — the judge ruling that **11 of 17** articles (mostly opinion pieces and interviews with democrats) had "**seditious intent**" — and **sentenced on 26 September 2024**: Chung to **21 months**, Lam to **11 months** (released immediately on medical grounds and time served over the two-year trial). The parent company, **Best Pencil**, was convicted and fined. Press-freedom groups called it a watershed: *"journalists jailed for doing their job."* Stand News's archive is preserved here: [[Stand News|sites.standnews]].

## The newest front — criminalising the reporter (2026)

On **30 September 2026**, national-security police arrested **Tang Ho-wing** (鄧浩榮, 37), who runs the online outlet **Boom News** (爆炸頭; some **200,000 followers**), and former League of Social Democrats member **Lee Ying-chi** (58), for allegedly "**spreading false information**" with **seditious intent** under the 2024 security law — an offence carrying up to **seven years**; the force confirmed the arrests on **1 October**. The arrests stemmed from an **31 August 2026** gathering outside **Prince Edward MTR station**, where people were found "holding bouquets and shouting slogans" to mark the **2019 Prince Edward incident** — the night riot police stormed a train and beat passengers, an event the authorities now call a "manipulated lie." Tang had posted video from the scene. Boom News's Facebook presence is preserved in this archive as a browsable web capture — see [[Boom News|sites.boomnews]].

Police said those involved were "suspected of spreading false information and attacking government with lies" to "incite hatred." The **Hong Kong Journalists Association** responded that "**reporting is not sedition**," warning that journalists now face arrest simply for covering public events; the **Committee to Protect Journalists** called it "**the latest sign of the criminalisation of journalism**" and demanded the pair's release ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/10/01/hong-kong-confirms-journalists-arrest-for-alleged-seditious-acts-linked-to-2019-prince-edward-mtr-incident-commemorations/)).

Tang was **released on bail shortly after midnight on 2 October**, after almost two days in custody; **no charge has been laid**, and the HKJA — "deeply concerned" — demanded that police disclose exactly which of his actions broke the law. He is one of **eight people** held over the 31 August gathering — three arrested on 3 September, three more on 27–28 September, and Tang and Lee on the 30th; the earlier six were freed on bail, and police have not ruled out further arrests ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/10/02/independent-hk-journalist-tang-ho-wing-released-on-bail-following-sedition-arrest/)). The case marks the frontier moving from the big newsrooms to a lone operator with a phone and a following.

Then the pressure moved from his reporting to his livelihood. On **7 October**, Tang said all of his **personal bank accounts had been frozen** — no advance notice, no formal freezing order shown — leaving him on cash, unable to take even food-delivery work, and, in his words, facing having to "resort to begging." No bank was named and no amount disclosed, and the authorities did not confirm ordering the freeze. It was first reported by the exile outlet **Points Media** (棱角媒體) and documented by the China Media Project's *[Lingua Sinica](https://lingua-sinica.org/frozen-out)*. Freezing the everyday banking of a journalist who has been charged with nothing echoes the asset and funding measures aimed at exiles abroad (see [[🌏 Pursued Abroad|pursued-abroad]]) — the same logic of cutting off money, now turned on someone still in the city.

## The weapons

- **The colonial sedition law.** A dormant offence under the old **Crimes Ordinance** (ss. 9–10), untouched since the 1960s, was revived from 2020 to prosecute speech, slogans, children's books and journalism alike.
- **Article 23 / the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance (2024).** Hong Kong's own security law, enacted 23 March 2024, re-enacted and **expanded sedition** — raising the maximum from two years to **seven** (ten where an "external force" is involved) and widening what counts as seditious intent.
- **The National Security Law (2020).** Beijing-imposed; the basis for the *Apple Daily* collusion case and the detention of [[Jimmy Lai|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]].
- **Money — tax audits and frozen accounts.** Pressure need not go through a courtroom. From **May 2025** the **Inland Revenue Department** ran simultaneous tax audits and backdated demands against at least **six outlets** (including HKFP) and some **20 linked individuals**; HKFP settled for **HK$57,692** after a 20-month probe (with a 135% penalty surcharge), and inMediaHK — found to owe nothing — still spent **HK$40,000** contesting it. On **13 April 2026** the **Hong Kong Journalists Association**, chaired by **Selina Cheng**, was ordered to pre-pay **HK$730,000** in provisional tax "within two days," more than double the previous year's HK$300,000. Cheng said the media audits divert resources from genuine high-value evaders and amount to "undue stress and unfair punishment," echoing tactics used elsewhere to charge journalists with tax offences "to undermine their credibility"; Commissioner Benjamin Chan denied the department weighs a taxpayer's occupation ([HKFP, 4 May 2026](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/05/04/hong-kong-press-union-faces-hk730k-prepaid-tax-demand-accuses-tax-office-of-misallocating-public-resources/)). The same financial squeeze reached individuals: [[Boom News|sites.boomnews]]' **Tang Ho-wing** had all his personal bank accounts frozen days after his bail release.

Together these turned editorial judgement — which article to run, which gathering to film — into potential evidence of a crime, while the tax office and the banks squeezed the outlets and journalists that remained. The same tools reach the archive's pages on [[book censorship|book-censorship]], the [[Tiananmen vigil|tiananmen-vigil]] and [[Glory to Hong Kong|glory-to-hong-kong]].

Hong Kong's civil-society websites, independent newsrooms and public memory are vanishing — some taken offline overnight, others quietly self-censored out of existence. **SHKO (Save Hong Kong Online)** is a community effort to preserve them before they disappear, and it runs on volunteers. You don't need to be an engineer to help: a single photograph, a memory, or a flagged link all add to the record.

This project is **anonymous, open source, and global**. Everything lives in a public repository that anyone can read, copy, and contribute to.

> ⚠️ **Before anything else, read [Protect yourself](#protect-yourself) below.** Preserving this material can carry real risk. Please take a moment to understand it and to shield your identity first.

## How to contribute via GitHub

The archive is kept in a public, open-source repository on GitHub:

**→ [github.com/China-Digital-Times-CDT/wepreserve](https://github.com/China-Digital-Times-CDT/wepreserve)**

Pick the right channel — each link opens a ready-made form:

| To… | Use |
|---|---|
| 📸 **Offer material** (photos, documents, oral history) | [Open a submission issue](https://github.com/China-Digital-Times-CDT/wepreserve/issues/new?template=01-submit-material.md) |
| 🔗 **Flag a site at risk** | [Open an at-risk-site issue](https://github.com/China-Digital-Times-CDT/wepreserve/issues/new?template=02-flag-at-risk-site.md) |
| 🗝️ **Request a restricted / unpublished archive** (licence or permission still pending) | [Open an access-request issue](https://github.com/China-Digital-Times-CDT/wepreserve/issues/new?template=03-request-restricted-archive.md) |
| 🐞 **Report a problem** (dead/rot link, broken image, replay viewer, layout, a factual error) | [Open a bug report](https://github.com/China-Digital-Times-CDT/wepreserve/issues/new?template=04-bug-report.md) |
| ✍️ **Fix or add content** | [Open a pull request](https://github.com/China-Digital-Times-CDT/wepreserve/pulls) — pages are plain Markdown in `vault/`, images in `vault/assets/` |

- **Why "request a restricted archive"?** Some material is **preserved but not yet publicly served** — the licence or a rights-holder's permission is still pending, or publishing it could expose people. Ask via the access-request form and we'll tell you what's possible.
- **Attaching sensitive files?** You can attach images and files to an issue, but if you'd rather not do so in public, just describe the material and we'll arrange a private channel.
- **No GitHub account?** Creating one takes a minute — see the safety notes below on doing so anonymously.

Not sure where something fits? [Open a blank issue](https://github.com/China-Digital-Times-CDT/wepreserve/issues/new) and ask. Every contribution is reviewed before it goes live, so nothing you send publishes automatically.

## Protect yourself

Preserving politically sensitive material from Hong Kong can carry legal and personal risk, especially under the National Security Law. Please take these precautions:

- **Understand the risk.** Only contribute what you are comfortable contributing, and think through your own exposure first.
- **Separate your identity.** Use a dedicated, **anonymous GitHub account** — not one tied to your real name, phone number, or main email. Consider a fresh email alias (e.g. a privacy-focused provider) for it.
- **Hide your connection.** Use **Tor** or a trusted **VPN** when submitting, so your IP isn't logged against the contribution.
- **Strip metadata from files.** Photos and documents can carry hidden GPS coordinates, device IDs, and timestamps. Remove EXIF/metadata before uploading, and crop out anything that could identify you or bystanders.
- **Talk securely.** For any private conversation, use an encrypted messenger such as **Signal** rather than plain email or SMS.
- **Don't self-incriminate.** Leave out details that reveal where you were or who you were with unless they're essential to the record and safe to share.

> When in doubt, share less about *yourself* and more about the *material*. The goal is to preserve the heritage without putting the people who saved it at risk.

## Who we are

SHKO is a decentralised, volunteer-run preservation project supported by a global network of contributors and partner organisations, including the Internet Archive, the Wikimedia Foundation, the Filecoin Foundation, Starling Lab, and China Digital Times. There is no central office and no membership roll — just people who believe Hong Kong's digital memory is worth keeping. You're welcome to join them.

## 2026-10 — Hong Kong Fire 2025 collection restructuring

**Status:** in progress · Milestone [HK Fire collection restructuring](https://github.com/China-Digital-Times-CDT/wepreserve/milestone/3) · Tracking issue [#30](https://github.com/China-Digital-Times-CDT/wepreserve/issues/30)

**Why.** The [[🔥 Hong Kong Fire 2025|hong-kong-fire-2025]] collection grew into the archive's largest, and parts became hard to scan. A measurement on 30 Oct 2026:

Parent: [[🔥 Hong Kong Fire 2025|hong-kong-fire-2025]] On **26 November 2025**, a fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po killed **168 people** — Hong Kong's deadliest fire since 1948. This page exists to hold their names. ## Who they were The dead were **58 men and 110 women**, aged from **six months to 98 years**. Among them were **one firefighter** (senior fireman Ho Wai-ho), **two renovation workers**, **five construction workers**, and **ten foreign domestic helpers** — women from Indonesia and the Philippines who died alongside the families they worked for. **Thirty-seven households lost at least two members.** By 15 January 2026 all 168 had been identified through forensic work, and every missing-person case was resolved. ## The names were almost never told For months after the fire the government **did not release the victims' names**. On 15 January 2026 the Secretary for Security said the names would be withheld "to respect the wishes of the bereaved"; Ming Pao reported that some families had not been asked whether they consented. The names entered the public record only on **10 June 2026**, when prosecutors charged seven people and two firms over the deaths and **read all 168 names into the court record** in the charge sheet. ## Pre-2025 Context

### Historical Fires
- **1948** A warehouse fire in Hong Kong killed 176 people, the deadliest fire in the city's recorded history (SCMP via [AP](https://apnews.com/article/hong-kong-tai-po-wang-fuk-court-fire-a84627d7f3ee62050c36a9aa3218205c)).
- **1996** A commercial building fire in Kowloon killed 41 people ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/hong-kong-tai-po-wang-fuk-court-fire-a84627d7f3ee62050c36a9aa3218205c)).

### Building Maintenance Industry
- **2012** Hong Kong introduces mandatory inspections for private buildings of 3+ stories that have reached 30 years and have other risk factors; ~600 buildings issued notices annually. Experts say the law is among the strictest in the world for governing high-rises but created pressure on a system vulnerable to corruption ([Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2025-12-30/hong-kong-fire-reveals-corruption-in-city-s-renovation-industry)).
- **2015** Hong Kong's first bid-rigging conviction: court documents describe a scheme devised at a dinner party in Shenzhen where a consultant, contractor, and homeowners' committee member agreed to use "shadow companies" to submit "pig quotes" (dummy bids). A middleman sentenced to 35 months for conspiracy to offer bribes totaling ~HK$45 million. Judge Josiah Lam warned that bid-rigging allowed contractors to "further lower the quality of a project" and "maximize exorbitant profits," flagging safety risks from lack of competition and oversight ([Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2025-12-30/hong-kong-fire-reveals-corruption-in-city-s-renovation-industry)).
- **2023–2025** Competition Commission and ICAC crackdowns dismantle at least 4 bid-rigging syndicates involved in 70+ renovation projects worth HK$2.3 billion ([Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2025-12-30/hong-kong-fire-reveals-corruption-in-city-s-renovation-industry)).
- **2025-09** Competition Commission raids offices of 9 contractors in connection with alleged bid-rigging involving 25 projects worth HK$600 million; describes two syndicates as "sizable" with "cohesive organizational structures" that had been "operating for some time" ([Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2025-12-30/hong-kong-fire-reveals-corruption-in-city-s-renovation-industry)).

### Wang Fuk Court Background
- **2017** FactWire publishes a building-maintenance bidding database (~3,000 bids across 220 estates) showing widespread bid-rigging patterns—context for later Wang Fuk Court tender concerns [FactWire](https://www.dotdotnews.com/a/202512/01/AP692d69ede4b0c32d4f618e05.html).
- **2023** After the MBIS tender is set, projected costs rise from ~HK$140m to HK$330m; residents allege bid-rigging and report suspected triad-linked figures blocking dissenting owners from meetings. A new owners' corporation replaces the old one in Sep 2024 but the contract is already signed (RFI).
- **2024-05-17** Contractor and whistleblower Jason Poon (Pan Zhuohong) reports use of non-compliant scaffolding netting at Wang Fuk Court, recording videos and sending multiple emails to the Fire Services Director; concerns reportedly not acted on.
- **2024-07** Owners' briefing on the HK$330m repair: residents object to rushed scope and lack of consultation; a lawyer warns that stopping the contract after a committee change could trigger owner liability. Residents say they tipped ICAC before contract signing but were told to supply evidence and saw no probe ([i-Cable](https://www.i-cable.com/%E6%96%B0%E8%81%9E%E8%B3%87%E8%A8%8A/415811/%E4%B8%80%E7%B7%9A%E6%90%9C%E6%9F%A5-%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E5%A4%A7%E7%81%AB%E8%83%8C%E5%BE%8C-%E4%B8%89%E7%96%91%E9%BB%9E%E6%83%B9%E9%97%9C%E6%B3%A8-%E5%B1%85%E6%B0%91)).
- **2024-09** Residents complain to the Labor Department about flammable scaffolding netting and foam boards sealing windows; department initially says netting not regulated, later cites contractor certificates and notes 16 inspections with notices/prosecutions but allows works to continue [NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/28/world/asia/hong-kong-fire-officials-warned.html).

## Timeline

**How to read this:** one chronological timeline split into **phases**. Each phase shows only the *lanes* (columns) active in it — lanes switch **on** as new strands emerge and **retire** when they no longer apply. Lanes: 🕯️ mourning / victims · 🔍 investigation / recovery · 🏠 resettlement / administrator · 💰 donations / insurance / budgets · ⚖️ legal / prosecutions / repression. Dense detail lives in the companion notes: [[hong-kong-fire-2025.investigation]] · [[hong-kong-fire-2025.activism]] · [[hong-kong-fire-2025.people]].

### Phase 1 — The Fire (Nov 26–27, 2025)

| Date | 🔥 The fire |
|------|-------------|
| **11-26** ~2:52 pm | Fire reported at Wang Fuk Court, Tai Po; escalated to **No. 5 alarm**. Outbreak on **Wang Cheong House** scaffolding, spreading to Wang Tai, Wang Shing, Wang Yan; by ~7:30 pm **7 of 8 towers** ablaze, only **Wang Chi House** spared ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/news/2025/nov/27/how-hong-kong-fire-unfolded-apartment-block-blaze-wang-court), [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/graphics/HONGKONG-FIRE/SPREAD/mopabqnzqva/)). A mid-floor doorbell cam shows the corridor smoke-filled by 3:00 pm with **no alarm sounding**; the resident fled by lift ([HK01](https://www.hk01.com/%E7%AA%81%E7%99%BC/60299887/%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E5%A4%A7%E7%81%AB-9%E5%88%86%E9%90%98%E7%85%99%E6%94%BB%E5%AE%8F%E6%98%8C%E9%96%A3%E8%B5%B0%E5%BB%8A-%E4%BD%8F%E6%88%B6%E6%90%AD%F0%A8%8B%A2%E9%80%83-%E7%8C%B6%E8%B1%AB3%E5%88%86%E9%90%98%E6%88%96%E7%84%A1%E5%91%BD)). |
| **11-26** | 800+ firefighters/paramedics mobilised; stairwell rescues in heavy smoke; **one firefighter** (Ho Wai-ho) later confirmed dead. Officials cite flammable **polystyrene** blocking windows ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/news/2025/nov/27/how-hong-kong-fire-unfolded-apartment-block-blaze-wang-court)). |
| **11-27** | Bamboo scaffolding and green netting spread flames; foam panels blew out windows. 200 trucks / 100 ambulances; ~**4,600 residents** across ~2,000 flats; 900+ in shelters; HK$300m fund announced; **no alarms** heard in any tower ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/news/2025/nov/27/how-hong-kong-fire-unfolded-apartment-block-blaze-wang-court), [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/graphics/HONGKONG-FIRE/SPREAD/mopabqnzqva/)). |

## Analysis & Commentary

### Fire Spread & Technical Analysis

- **2025-12-02** BBC visual guide maps spread: traces fire origin to Wang Cheong House, spread to six more blocks within ~90 minutes, notes 44-hour suppression to 10:18 a.m. Nov 28, alarms failing in all eight towers, and highlights flammable foam boards/netting and bamboo scaffold collapse contributing to propagation (BBC visual explainer).
- **2025-12-02** Grenfell inquiry expert José Luis Torero tells HKEJ/Yahoo the blaze resembles Grenfell in vertical spread and smoke overrunning escape routes; suspects combustible foam/polystyrene cladding and channel-flow between towers as main drivers rather than bamboo alone; calls for a Grenfell-level technical probe into materials, compartmentation, spacing, and smoke-path failure ([Yahoo/信報](https://hk.finance.yahoo.com/news/%E8%8B%B1%E7%81%AB%E7%81%BD%E8%AA%BF%E6%9F%A5%E5%B0%88%E5%AE%B6-%E5%88%B6%E5%BA%A6%E5%A4%B1%E6%95%88%E7%8C%9B%E6%96%BC%E7%81%AB-2017%E5%80%AB%E6%95%A6%E4%BD%8F%E5%AE%85%E5%A4%A7%E5%BB%88%E7%87%92%E9%80%9A%E9%A0%82-%E8%88%87%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E7%9B%B8%E4%BC%BC-184700834.html)).
- **2025-12-09** Feature in Taiwanese outlet Tian Jian spotlights Hong Kong voices saying bamboo scapegoating distracts from oversight and bid-rigging failures; recounts misinformation corrections by PolyU's Xinyan Huang and ReNews ([Tian Jian](https://tian-jian.org/hong-kong-tai-po-wang-fuk-court-fire/)).

### Political & Systemic Analysis

- **2025-12-02** Global Voices opinion argues negligence and MBIS oversight failures—not bamboo—drove the disaster; cites HK$330m tender controversies, ignored complaints about flammable netting/foam, 43-hour burn, and suppression of calls for an independent investigation (Global Voices).
- **2025-12-02** AP analysis flags "tip of an iceberg": notes 7 of 20 net samples failed, cost-cutting net swaps after a typhoon, alarms not sounding, and suspension of 28 other projects by the same contractor; political analysts warn of systemic bid-rigging/oversight gaps and national-security arrests of petition organizers amid public anger ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/hong-wang-china-dissent-fire-construction-ff953aec2bc0201b0e3255805a241fc1)).
- **2025-12-02** Foreign Policy column says the fire underscores Hong Kong's loss of freedoms: authorities suppressed civil aid and detained petitioners; independent inquiries like Grenfell's are now impossible under NSL, making Hong Kong's response mirror the mainland ([Foreign Policy](https://foreignpolicy.com/2025/12/02/hong-kong-apartment-fire-china-political-freedoms/)).
- **2025-12-13** The Atlantic argues bamboo scapegoating misses systemic causes: elite-contractor collusion and deregulated housing markets since 1997, flammable foam/window cladding and non-compliant netting, possible alarm deactivation, and suppressed petitions/mourning (sedition arrests, campus poster removals, media "warning" meeting); warns Hong Kong is moving toward Beijing-style repression with low-turnout "patriots-only" elections ([The Atlantic](https://www.theatlantic.com/international/2025/12/hong-kong-fire-investigation/685204/)).
- **2025-12-30** Bloomberg publishes a feature on corruption in Hong Kong's billion-dollar renovation industry, citing crackdowns since 2023 that dismantled at least 4 bid-rigging syndicates involved in 70+ projects worth HK$2.3 billion. Profiles anti-bid-rigging activist Chiu Yan-loy (Property Owners Anti-Bid Rigging Alliance), who has campaigned for two decades. Notes that residents at Sui Wo Court (near Wang Fuk Court) gathered every weekend since early 2025 to protest a HK$371 million renovation, while Fairview Park (Yuen Long) residents marched to ICAC after the fire to demand investigation of a HK$500 million pipe replacement project. ICAC tells Bloomberg it is pursuing a "three-pronged strategy of law enforcement, systemic prevention and community education." Whistleblower Jason Poon: "It's no longer just about one estate, it's about whether the entire building-maintenance system has been compromised" ([Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2025-12-30/hong-kong-fire-reveals-corruption-in-city-s-renovation-industry)).

What happens to the ~2,000 flats and their owners after the fire is a story of its own: a government buyback of the seven ruined blocks, a long fight by owners for a statutory meeting with the government-appointed administrator, and the scramble for somewhere to live. This page gathers that thread. For the people living through it, see the displaced-resident profiles on [[hong-kong-fire-2025.people]]; for the dated sequence, [[hong-kong-fire-2025.timeline]].

## The buyback scheme

- **The plan (21 Feb 2026).** The government offered to buy back flats in the **seven fire-damaged blocks** at **HK$8,000/sq ft** (without land premium) or **HK$10,500/sq ft** (with), with **flat-for-flat** exchanges available from 10 Home Ownership Scheme / Housing Society projects. **Wang Chi House** — the one block largely spared — was initially excluded. **Redevelopment was ruled out**, the government citing a 9–10-year timeline ([SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/society/article/3344228/wang-fuk-court-buyback-plan-disappoints-some-residents-despite-generous-offer)).
- **The money (25 Feb 2026 Budget).** HK$4b public funds + HK$2.8b from the Support Fund = **HK$6.8b** earmarked. An early survey found **74%** would consider acquisition and **9%** insisted on redevelopment only.
- **Offer letters (14 May 2026)** went out at the HK$8,000–10,500/sq ft terms, with a **75% acceptance threshold** and a flat-selection deadline of **30 June**.
- **Hop On** (the administrator) began **refunding ~HK$127m** of the renovation fund that had financed the deadly works.

### Rehousing options
Transitional and permanent rehousing was spread across several estates and years: **Shing Chi Court** (Kowloon Bay, from **Sep 2026**); **Kam Tin Wui Hei Court** (late **Aug 2027**); and new Tai Po developments at **Chung Nga Road West** (**2029**) and **Kwong Fuk Park** (**2033**). Many displaced residents are elderly and wanted to stay in Tai Po; the long timelines pushed some to accept flats in other districts (see the profiles on [[hong-kong-fire-2025.people]]).

## Uptake — and the 17 holdouts

- Over **85%** of fire-hit-block owners had accepted by the **30 June** flat-selection deadline.
- By the **31 August** deadline, **99.1% (1,967 of 1,984)** had accepted — leaving **17 holdouts**, who face **compulsory acquisition**, with compensation likely pegged to the lower post-fire value and enabling legislation flagged for **2027**.
- **Wang Chi House** (the spared block) was brought in with a separate **~HK$1b** offer (extended in June): by **21 August**, **91.5%** of its owners had accepted and **67.7%** had signed sale-and-purchase agreements, against a **15 October** signing deadline (the final tally is not yet reported).

## The fight for a homeowners' meeting

After the fire, the government installed **Hop On Management** (a Chinachem subsidiary) as the estate's administrator. Owners spent months trying to force a statutory general meeting to get answers on funds, insurance and their future housing — and were repeatedly blocked.

- **Online petition → forgery referral (5–10 Apr 2026).** Owners gathered a petition (**428 valid** signatures, above the 5% Building Management Ordinance threshold of ~100 of 1,984 units) to compel a general meeting. Hop On **rejected** it on **5 April**; on **10 April** the Home Affairs Department **referred the petition to law enforcement**, alleging it "lacked authentication mechanisms and may involve people impersonating owners and forging signatures" ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/04/10/tai-po-fire-owners-petition-for-meeting-with-estate-administrator-may-contain-forged-signatures-govt-says/)).
- **Owners regroup (29 Apr 2026).** Undeterred, owners delivered **247 handwritten** signatures (~12% of households). Under the BMO this obliged Hop On to issue a meeting notice within 14 days (by **14 May**) and hold the meeting within 45 days ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/05/14/tai-po-fire-administrator-of-fire-hit-wang-fuk-court-seeks-to-extend-deadline-for-homeowners-meeting/)).
- **The administrator stalls (14–20 May 2026).** On the notice deadline, Hop On instead asked the **Lands Tribunal to extend** the statutory timeframe, citing signature verification and venue logistics, and held **online-only "information sessions"** (from 20 May) with **no voting** and reported registration glitches ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/05/11/tai-po-fire-wang-fuk-court-residents-hit-registration-hurdles-for-online-meeting-with-management-firm/)).
- **Tribunal rejects the delay (1–2 Jun 2026).** Lands Tribunal Judge **Gary Lam denied** the postponement: there was **no jurisdiction** under the BMO to vary the timeframe, and delay would infringe owners' right to a meeting — Hop On already held contact details for **1,601 of 1,984** owners, so the difficulty was "not insurmountable" ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/06/02/tai-po-fire-court-denies-estate-administrators-bid-to-postpone-owners-meeting/)).
- **Government backs the administrator (9 Jun 2026).** CE **John Lee defended Hop On** over the delay, drawing criticism that officials were shielding the administrator rather than enforcing the meeting owners had demanded since March ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/06/09/tai-po-fire-hong-kong-leader-defends-housing-estate-administrator-over-owners-meeting-delay/)).
- **First statutory meeting (19 Jul 2026).** The meeting finally convened across **four venues**. Owners **rejected Hop On's audit report** but backed holding a second meeting within two months.

## Belongings retrieval (20 Apr – 4 May 2026)

Announced by Deputy Chief Secretary **Warner Cheuk** (卓永興) on 27 March, retrieval ran in **3-hour slots**, stairs only, **max four people per flat**, with **1,000 personnel** deployed. On day one (Wang Sun House, 1F–10F), **264 of 267** registered residents attended; average stay 1h 44min; one resident in his 70s was hospitalised with breathing difficulty and discharged the same day; of 11 missing-item reports, 4 were recovered, 4 judged destroyed, and 3 placed under police investigation ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/03/27/wang-fuk-court-residents-to-get-3-hour-slots-to-retrieve-belongings-at-fire-hit-estate-from-mid-april/), [The Witness](https://thewitnesshk.com/%e5%ae%8f%e7%a6%8f%e8%8b%91%e5%b1%85%e6%b0%91%e9%a6%96%e6%97%a5%e5%9b%9e%e5%ae%b6-%e9%a6%96%e6%89%b9%e9%96%8b%e6%94%be%e5%ae%8f%e6%96%b0%e9%96%a3-%e5%a4%a7%e5%9f%94%e7%8f%be%e5%a0%b4%e7%9b%b4%e6%93%8a/)).

## Relief payments

Separate from the buyback, a government-led **Wang Fuk Court Assistance Fund** (~HK$2.3b: ~HK$2b donations + HK$300m government seed) made emergency disbursements: **HK$200,000 condolence** and **HK$50,000 funeral** per fatality, and **HK$50,000 living allowance** per affected household (announced by Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs **Alice Mak**). For the corporate and philanthropic donation roster, see **Donations and Aid** on [[hong-kong-fire-2025.activism]].

Parent: [[hong-kong-fire-2025]] On **22 October 2026** the judge-led Independent Committee submitted its final report on the Wang Fuk Court fire to Chief Executive John Lee. A **redacted public version was released on 29 October 2026** — and the same day the government staged its reckoning: Lee led seven officials in a bow of apology, one bureau chief resigned, and a package of reforms was announced. This page collects the report itself (with preserved copies), what it withholds and why, and what the government did when it landed. ## What the report is - **Two volumes, 16 chapters.** The English edition runs to **1,208 pages** (Volume 1: 505 pp; Volume 2: 703 pp); the report was also published in Traditional and Simplified Chinese. Authored by **The Hon. Mr Justice David Lok**, **Mr Chan Kin-por** and **Dr Rex Auyeung**, dated October 2026. - **A searchable record, not a scan.** The published PDFs carry a full text layer, so the public version can be read and searched in full — valuable for preservation. - **Released by the government, hosted by the committee.** The redacted version sits on the committee's own site; the government announced the release on 29 October ([committee report page](https://www.ic-wangfukcourtfire.gov.hk/eng/report.html); [government release](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202610/29/P2026102900343.htm)). ## What is redacted — and why it matters The front page of each volume carries the same notice: > "With a view to avoiding any prejudice (actual or perceived) to the relevant criminal prosecutions, certain parts of the Index, Executive Summary and Chapters 4, 6, 10 to 15 of the main body of this Report have been redacted." The notice says **certain parts** of these sections are redacted — not that the chapters are gone. All of the listed chapters that we checked (4, 6 and 11–15) are present in the published volumes with their body text, including Chapter 6 on the causes of the fire and Chapter 11 on the responsibility and accountability of government bodies. The Standard counted **passages redacted on more than 40 of the 1,013 pages** (two volumes, 16 chapters and nine annexes), mostly in Chapters 10 and 11, with 34 redactions in the section on contractors' responsibilities ([The Standard](https://thestandard.com.hk/news/article/346969/Wang-Fuk-Court-report-released-with-passages-redacted-on-more-than-40-pages-govt-cites-criminal-proceedings)). The archive has not yet mapped these itself. | Chapters the notice lists as having redacted parts | Chapters the notice does not list | | --- | --- | | Ch 4 — Building maintenance & renovation works · Ch 6 — Causes of the fire, fire spread and heavy casualties · Ch 10 — Responsibilities of the contractors · Ch 11 — Responsibility and accountability of government bodies · Ch 12–15 — Recommendations, bid-rigging and anti-competitive conduct | Ch 1–3 — Introduction, scope, description of the estate · Ch 5 — The day of the fire · Ch 7 — Firefighting and evacuation · Ch 8 — The death of Senior Fireman Ho Wai-ho · Ch 9 — Regulatory regimes · Ch 16 — Conclusion | Chapter 4 itself explains the division of labour: it sets out facts, while "the responsibilities of various stakeholders are examined in Chapters 10 and 11" — two of the chapters the notice lists as partly redacted. **The full report already exists** — it was handed to the Chief Executive unredacted on 22 October. The redactions are tied to the live prosecutions (seven people and two firms face charges including manslaughter), and the government says the full report will be released once all related criminal proceedings have ended ([The Standard](https://thestandard.com.hk/news/article/346969/Wang-Fuk-Court-report-released-with-passages-redacted-on-more-than-40-pages-govt-cites-criminal-proceedings)). Until then, this redacted version is the record — and if even it is ever taken down or further trimmed, a preserved copy becomes the archive's treasure. (See [Preserved copies](#preserved-copies) below.) ## The apology — and the single resignation When the redacted report was released on 29 October, at the very start of the press conference **Chief Executive John Lee led seven senior officials in a formal bow of apology** to the victims and the public. > **On sourcing this image.** These are stills from the government's *own* press-conference webcast (ISD) — official footage of its own officials, credited to the Information Services Department. The widely-circulated agency photographs of the same moment (AP, Reuters) are **not** rehosted here, in keeping with the archive's rule against reusing news-agency photos. Only **one official was held politically accountable: Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho** (何永賢). She offered her resignation on 28 October; Lee accepted it, began the process of asking Beijing to formally remove her, and named Deputy Financial Secretary **Michael Wong** (黃偉綸) as acting housing chief. The logic: the **Independent Checking Unit** — found to bear the heaviest responsibility among four faulted government bodies — sits under her bureau. Lee framed holding a single official to account as **"my personal political decision,"** a line widely criticised as too little when the committee faulted four departments (the ICU, the Fire Services, Buildings and Labour Departments). Before the release, Executive Council member Ronny Tong had floated a "no-fault, no-accountability" framing. Separately, the **Public Service Commission formed an Investigation Team** to examine the individual responsibilities of the civil servants who oversaw the fire-risk aspects of the works ([government release](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202610/29/P2026102900644.htm)) ([BBC中文](https://www.bbc.com/zhongwen/articles/c95ynv03lmk8o/trad); [HKFP: Ho to step down](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/10/29/breaking-housing-chief-winnie-ho-to-step-down-over-wang-fuk-court-blaze-almost-1-year-after-tragedy-that-killed-168/)). ## The demands for more resignations Winnie Ho's departure did not settle the question. The report faulted four bodies, each under a different minister, and **three of those ministers stayed**. Bereaved residents want all four gone, and reporters pressed the three repeatedly on 29 and 30 October. | Minister | Body faulted | Response when asked about resigning | | --- | --- | --- | | **Winnie Ho** (何永賢), Housing | Independent Checking Unit | **Resigned.** Absent from the press conference; her statement accepted political responsibility but did not apologise. | | **Chris Tang** (鄧炳強), Security | Fire Services Department | **Staying.** Pressed repeatedly on 30 Oct: "I'm not important. Society is important, Hong Kong is important, the country is important." | | **Bernadette Linn** (甯漢豪), Development | Buildings Department | **Staying.** Said she **had thought about resigning**, but likened herself to crew who must follow the captain. Would not say whether she had offered to go. | | **Chris Sun** (孫玉菡), Labour and Welfare | Labour Department | **Staying.** Did not directly answer whether he had considered resigning, or whether he would donate his salary as another form of accountability. | **What the bereaved and residents are asking.** - **Yip Ka-kui** (葉家駒), whose wife died in the fire, called one resignation a restaurant's "**minimum charge**" and said the ministers over all four faulted bodies should step down: "I will not accept it." He also said Ho should have apologised in person if she truly accepted responsibility. - **Lee Kwok-hung** (李國鴻), who lost his mother and two domestic workers: "It wasn't just one department that made mistakes... Why is only one minister bearing the consequences?" - **Betty Ho**, a resident, said Ho resigned rather than being sacked, and asked how that amounted to accountability: "She has just quit her job." - **Phyllis Lo**, who lost her mother, said one official stepping down, voluntarily rather than as a penalty, was not enough, and that justice had not yet been done. Not all residents agreed: one surnamed Tam told TVB he had not expected any senior official to resign and urged people not to focus on why only one had gone ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/10/30/some-wang-fuk-court-survivors-say-top-officials-apology-nearly-one-year-since-fatal-fire-lacked-sincerity); [The Witness](https://thewitnesshk.com/%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E5%A4%A7%E7%81%AB%E5%A0%B1%E5%91%8A%E5%B1%85%E6%B0%91%E8%A7%80%E7%9C%8B%E8%A8%98%E8%80%85%E6%9C%83%E8%BD%89%E6%92%AD-%E8%B3%AA%E7%96%91%E9%AB%98%E5%AE%98%E9%81%93%E6%AD%89/); [太報](https://www.taisounds.com/news/content/84/296899)). **The government's answer.** John Lee called it his "**personal political decision**", based on each official's role, their subordinates' performance and the work ahead, and said the three must follow it and carry out the reforms. Asked about his own accountability, he said that as the person with first responsibility he must lead the government through the problems and the reforms ([The Witness](https://thewitnesshk.com/%e5%ae%8f%e7%a6%8f%e8%8b%91%e5%a4%a7%e7%81%ab%e5%95%8f%e8%b2%ac%e5%9c%98%e9%9a%8a%e5%83%85%e4%b8%80%e4%ba%ba%e8%ab%8b%e8%be%ad-%e5%85%ac%e5%8b%99%e5%93%a1%e7%b4%8450%e4%ba%ba%e5%8f%97%e6%9f%a5/); [The Witness: Linn and Sun](https://thewitnesshk.com/%e5%ae%8f%e7%a6%8f%e8%8b%91%e5%a4%a7%e7%81%ab%e7%94%af%e6%bc%a2%e8%b1%aa%e7%a8%b1%e6%80%9d%e8%80%83%e9%81%8e%e8%ab%8b%e8%be%ad-%e5%ad%ab%e7%8e%89%e8%8f%a1%e9%81%bf%e7%ad%94%e6%9c%83%e5%90%a6%e6%8d%90/); [The Witness: Tang](https://thewitnesshk.com/%e5%ae%8f%e7%a6%8f%e8%8b%91%e5%a4%a7%e7%81%ab%e5%a0%b1%e5%91%8a%e9%bb%9e%e5%90%8d%e6%89%b9%e6%b6%88%e9%98%b2%e8%99%95%e6%9c%89%e7%bc%ba%e5%a4%b1-%e9%84%a7%e7%82%b3%e5%bc%b7%e7%a8%b1%e9%83%a8%e9%96%80/)). **Who defended it.** Beijing's Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office praised the government's sense of responsibility and warned against those it accused of using the disaster to stir up discontent ([The Witness](https://thewitnesshk.com/%e5%ae%8f%e7%a6%8f%e8%8b%91%e5%a4%a7%e7%81%ab%e5%95%8f%e8%b2%ac%e5%9c%98%e9%9a%8a%e5%83%85%e4%b8%80%e4%ba%ba%e8%ab%8b%e8%be%ad-%e5%85%ac%e5%8b%99%e5%93%a1%e7%b4%8450%e4%ba%ba%e5%8f%97%e6%9f%a5/)). Executive Council member Ronny Tong and former NPC Standing Committee member Tam Yiu-chung also backed the outcome, HK01 reported ([HK01](https://www.hk01.com/%E6%94%BF%E6%83%85/60405043/%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E5%95%8F%E8%B2%AC-%E6%8B%86%E5%B1%80-%E4%BD%95%E6%B0%B8%E8%B3%A2%E4%B8%8B%E5%8F%B0%E6%9C%80%E5%A4%A7%E5%85%AC%E7%B4%84%E6%95%B8-%E5%85%AC%E5%83%95%E8%BF%BD%E8%B2%AC%E6%89%8D%E6%98%AF%E5%A4%A7%E5%9C%B0%E9%9C%87)). **What happens next: civil servants.** A separate Public Service Commission investigation is due within **three months**. It will treat about **40–50 civil servants** across the four bodies as subjects and involve about 100 overall. Penalties range from a warning to dismissal, and pensions can be withheld or cut for those about to retire ([The Witness](https://thewitnesshk.com/%e5%ae%8f%e7%a6%8f%e8%8b%91%e5%a4%a7%e7%81%ab%e5%95%8f%e8%b2%ac%e5%9c%98%e9%9a%8a%e5%83%85%e4%b8%80%e4%ba%ba%e8%ab%8b%e8%be%ad-%e5%85%ac%e5%8b%99%e5%93%a1%e7%b4%8450%e4%ba%ba%e5%8f%97%e6%9f%a5/)). Yip also says the inquiry's picture has "missing pieces", because some witnesses never testified, and that he will study the report with his lawyers ([The Witness](https://thewitnesshk.com/%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E5%A4%A7%E7%81%AB%E5%A0%B1%E5%91%8A%E5%B1%85%E6%B0%91%E8%A7%80%E7%9C%8B%E8%A8%98%E8%80%85%E6%9C%83%E8%BD%89%E6%92%AD-%E8%B3%AA%E7%96%91%E9%AB%98%E5%AE%98%E9%81%93%E6%AD%89/)). ## The reforms announced Alongside the report, the government set out a reform package, to be steered by a committee chaired by the Chief Secretary: - **Criminalise bid-rigging** in building maintenance — a bill targeted for the Legislative Council by year-end; the Competition Commission floated jail terms of 7–10 years. - **Scrap and replace the Independent Checking Unit**, criticised in the report for multiple failings and a "slack attitude." - Create a new **Building Maintenance Support and Services Authority** to help owners manage major renovation works. - Stand up a **cross-agency task force** (police, ICAC, Competition Commission) against collusion in maintenance projects. - Amend the **Buildings Ordinance** to end the industry's self-regulation and raise penalties. ([HKFP: new authority & bid-rigging offence](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/10/29/tai-po-fire-hong-kong-govt-to-set-up-company-to-assist-owners-with-building-renovations-criminalise-bid-rigging/); [HKFP: ICU to be replaced](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/10/29/tai-po-fire-housing-bureau-to-replace-inspection-unit-criticised-for-multiple-failings-slack-attitude/)). ## The families' verdict The bereaved were not placated. **Yip Ka-kui** (葉家駒) — whose wife **Bai Shui Lin** (白瑞蓮) died in the fire while helping neighbours escape — said he could not accept only one bureau chief stepping down: *every* policy secretary the report named should go, the heads of the **Fire Services and Labour Departments** included. He derided the government's selective accountability as refined to the "**nanometre grade**" — "when there's credit, the bureau chief shares in it; when something goes wrong, it's the people below who are at fault." Preventing a recurrence, he argued, demands "**reform of the whole system**" and an end to the departments' buck-passing (卸膊) culture, not patched-up clauses. **Mr So** (蘇先生), who lost both parents, had himself tried to raise the alarm — and his story is one of the **180 pre-fire complaints the report says six departments passed around** (see [[hong-kong-fire-2025.investigation]]). In September 2024 he twice telephoned the **Fire Services Department** about the risk of the foam boards sealing the windows — invoking London's **Grenfell Tower** fire — only to be told there was no specific regulation on window-covering materials and to ask the **Buildings Department** instead. "A flammable thing stuck to the outside of your home — how is that not the fire service's concern?" he said; an ordinary resident cannot be expected to know the departments' division of labour. Even his father, in his eighties, had warned after a 2025 fire at Central's Wah Mau building that Wang Fuk's foam-sealed windows would be lethal. Like the others he rejected the lone resignation — Winnie Ho did not herself bow, and quitting is not the same as being held to account — and condemned the eleven-month wait for an apology ("investigation and apology do not conflict"). He wants the government to hold an **annual official memorial** as a formal admission of its failures. **Lee Kwok-hung** (李國鴻), who lost his mother and two domestic helpers, doubted the reforms would bite: pointing to earlier anti-collusion measures that failed to stop bid-rigging — a 2013 maintenance scheme and the Urban Renewal Authority's 2016 "招標妥" tender safeguard — he questioned whether the new Building Maintenance Support and Services Authority would do any better. The two spoke after the contractors' criminal case — **Prestige Construction**, **Will Power Architects** (鴻毅) and seven directors on 25 charges including manslaughter — was adjourned at West Kowloon Magistrates' Court to **14 January 2027** (Will Power, in liquidation, still had no legal representation) ([InMedia 獨立媒體](https://www.inmediahk.net/node/%E6%94%BF%E7%B6%93/%E3%80%90%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E4%BA%94%E7%B4%9A%E7%81%AB%E3%80%91%E9%81%BA%E5%B1%AC%E8%91%89%E5%AE%B6%E9%A7%92%EF%BC%9A%E4%B8%8D%E6%8E%A5%E5%8F%97%E5%83%85%E4%B8%80%E5%90%8D%E5%B1%80%E9%95%B7%E4%B8%8B%E5%8F%B0)). ## Preserved copies The archive keeps its own copy of all six published volumes, so the record survives even if the official copy is moved, taken down or further redacted.
