## Vigils and Mourning
- Three-day citywide mourning (Nov 29–Dec 1): flags at half-mast across government sites and overseas offices; condolence books open in all 18 districts; public hotlines for casualty inquiries and mental health support (SCMP).
- On-site memorials and note removals reported; residents continued placing messages nearby.
- Mourners at Wang Fuk Court displayed placards reading “要检讨嘅唔系竹棚 而系个制度” (“Review the system, not the bamboo”), rejecting attempts to blame bamboo scaffolding for the spread (RFI).
- WSJ described thousands gathering on Dec 1 to lay flowers and donate supplies; ad-hoc relief booths were later replaced by police command tents as authorities formalized the site ([WSJ](https://www.wsj.com/world/china/hong-kongs-response-to-deadly-fire-is-squeezed-by-chinas-firm-hand-ea01b5a2)).
- “頭七” memorial (Nov 30–Dec 2): Kowloon Funeral Parlour opened East Hall for three days for public mourning; projection screen displayed e-condolences, including calls for “公義” and “徹查真相.” Hundreds—students in uniform, nearby office workers—queued through lunch to lay flowers; sobbing and paper-offering folding reported despite weekday timing (local reports).
- Diaspora vigil (Dec 5): Hong Kongers in Britain (HKB) announced a London memorial 6–8:30 p.m. at 1 Coral Street, SE1 with altar, Lennon Wall and silent area; 200–300 attendees expected; organizers called for an open, transparent inquiry (Points Media).
- Diaspora vigil (Dec 6): a Toronto/North York memorial was announced for 4:30–5:30 p.m. at North York Memorial Community Hall, 5110 Yonge St, with doors open from 4:00 for flowers; a Lennon Wall and petition signing for an independent inquiry were to stay open afterward (Hong Kong-Canada Association via A1 Chinese Radio).
- Diaspora vigil (Dec 7): a community notice announced a New York prayer service at Transfiguration Church, 29 Mott Street, 4:00 p.m., with clergy to lead a benediction and hymn singing from 3:00 p.m.; an open invitation went out to mourn Wang Fuk Court victims.
- Diaspora vigil (Dec 6, Taipei): Taiwan-based Hongkongers announced a memorial at the Liberty Square/CKS Memorial Hall archway (No. 21, Zhongshan South Rd, Zhongzheng Dist., Taipei), 7:00–9:00 p.m.; flowers encouraged, message cards to be provided; languages: Cantonese/Mandarin/English (community call).
- Diaspora vigil (Dec 6, Auckland): a memorial was announced at Ellen Melville Centre, 2 Freyberg Place, 4:00–5:30 p.m.; black/neutral attire and flowers encouraged; with a vigil, Lennon Wall and petition planned (community call).

## Accountability and Detentions

*The sedition and national-security prosecutions below are part of the wider assault on Hong Kong's civic space and media — see the [[press-freedom]] hub.*

- Petitions/leaflets: Arrests of student Miles Kwan (關靖豐, petition >10k signatures), former district councillor Kenneth Cheung, and volunteer surnamed Li over accountability leaflets/messages (RFI/HKFP).
- CUHK expulsion (Feb 13, 2026): Miles Kwan disclosed on social media that CUHK notified him of expulsion. The university declined to comment on individual cases but stated that repeated violations or serious misconduct can result in expulsion, and students with three demerits are also expelled ([Now News](https://news.now.com/home/local/player?newsId=636762)).
- Petition clampdown: The Diplomat reports a student arrested for sedition after handing out flyers for a four-demand petition; friends relaunched the petition offshore, hitting ~11,900 signatures by Dec 4, citing safety concerns for onshore organizers ([The Diplomat](https://thediplomat.com/2025/12/hong-kongs-grenfell-tower-moment-when-grief-became-sedition/)).
- Protests/vigils calling for independent investigation; police/security officials warned against “misinformation.”
- Volunteer clampdown: ABC reported volunteers and NGOs distributing food and support were told to leave the site on Dec 1, reflecting official concern over gatherings; its “One fire, two systems” piece links the petition arrest and aid withdrawal to Beijing’s red lines on grief and accountability ([ABC](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-12-02/tai-po-fire-hong-kong-mainland-grief-red-lines/106087732)).
- Election context: Government said Dec 7 LegCo campaign activities would pause while authorities address the fire; activists’ online petition echoed 2019 protest demands, and rights groups warned the National Security Law chills discussion of the disaster (WSJ).
- Civil society presser (Dec 2) on high-rise repair policy canceled less than four hours before start after organizer Law Shing-lai (ADPL) met National Security police; HKFP reports solicitor and former ADPL chair Bruce Liu was taken in by the national security department ahead of the event. The agenda included resident support, an inquiry demand, potential bid-rigging/substandard materials, and regulator roles; slated speakers included ADPL’s Kwok Wai-shing and Jay Li plus town planner/former Democratic Party member Stanley Ng ([InMediaHK](https://www.inmediahk.net/node/%E6%94%BF%E7%B6%93/%E3%80%90%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E4%BA%94%E7%B4%9A%E7%81%AB%E3%80%91%E6%B0%91%E9%96%93%E8%A8%98%E8%80%85%E6%9C%83%E5%8F%96%E6%B6%88-%E5%BB%96%E6%88%90%E5%88%A9%E8%A2%AB%E5%9C%8B%E5%AE%89%E8%99%95%E9%82%80%E6%9C%83%E9%9D%A2%EF%BC%9A%E5%B7%B2%E7%B0%BD%E4%BF%9D%E5%AF%86%E5%8D%94%E8%AD%B0%E4%B8%8D%E8%83%BD%E9%80%8F%E9%9C%B2?utm_source=dable) [HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2025/12/02/hong-kong-solicitor-taken-in-by-nat-sec-police-as-civic-press-event-on-deadly-tai-po-blaze-axed/)).
- Campus censorship: Baptist University Students’ Union posted mourning posters on Dec 2 reading “沉痛哀悼宏福苑大火死者 / WE ARE HONGKONGERS / 懇請政府從善如流 回應公眾需求 公義得到伸張”; by the next day the university cordoned off the SU board and Democracy Wall with barriers, blocking access to the posters and sparking online criticism that even seeking truth is being curtailed ([Threads](https://www.threads.com/@kong.news/post/DRzA_zAEs3a)).
- Owners’ committee accountability: DAB-linked advisor Wong Bik-kiu vows police/ICAC reports over alleged misconduct and safety risks; highlights man-made disaster framing and calls for full accountability (DotDotNews/HK01).
- Public commentary on accountability: Threads posts highlight lack of official resignations after the death toll climbed past 150 with dozens unaccounted (an early-December 2025 figure; the confirmed final toll was 168) and cite AFP question to John Lee (“Can you tell us why you deserve to keep your job?”) ([Threads](https://www.threads.com/@kaminghk/post/DRxEWgCj7mz?xmt=AQF0Y8QlE4EeoRWNRx0-ZokkHaRfuw3I-2LSifPZ25bpOQ)).
- National security arrest (Dec 6): Police NSD arrested a 71-year-old man, reportedly commentator Wong On-yin, for alleged “obstructing national security investigation” under Article 88 and sedition after he posted content from a Dec 2 interview about the fire; police said the disclosure “tipped off” others ([Yahoo News HK](https://hk.news.yahoo.com/%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E4%BA%94%E7%B4%9A%E7%81%AB%EF%BD%9C%E5%9C%8B%E5%AE%89%E8%99%95%E6%8B%98-71-%E6%AD%B2%E7%94%B7%E5%AD%90-%E6%93%9A%E6%82%89%E7%82%BA%E8%A9%95%E8%AB%96%E4%BA%BA%E7%8E%8B%E5%B2%B8%E7%84%B6-%E9%A6%96%E5%BC%95%E7%94%A8%E7%AC%AC88%E6%A2%9D-%E6%9D%8E%E6%A1%82%E8%8F%AF%EF%BC%9A%E6%B6%89%E5%8A%A9%E6%9F%A5%E5%BE%8C%E5%85%AC%E9%96%8B%E5%85%A7%E5%AE%B9%EF%BD%9Cyahoo-114227522.html)).
- Court follow-up (Dec 9): The arrested commentator, named as Wong Kwok-ngon (pen name Wong On-yin), is charged with disclosing national security investigation details (first prosecution of the new Article 88 offence) and with sedition for Jan 3–Dec 6 YouTube videos; national security judge Victor So denies bail and remands him pending a Jan 20 hearing while police review ~2,400 videos and 15 seized devices ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2025/12/09/political-commentator-remanded-in-custody-after-being-charged-with-revealing-details-of-nat-sec-probe/)).
- Police annual review (Feb 11, 2026): Deputy Commissioner (National Security) Kan Kai-yan confirms multiple people arrested under national security laws over the fire; refuses to disclose total number. Three charged: (1) one for seditious publications (adjourned Feb 27); (2) Wong Kwok-ngon for seditious videos + obstructing national security investigation (adjourned Feb 23); (3) one for seditious publications (hearing Mar 4). Kan criticizes those who cited "force majeure" (不可抗力) to stop coverage—calling it "unfair" and "smearing" police—saying the real reasons included financial/resource issues or fear of breaking the law. Commissioner Chow Yat-ming warns of "soft resistance," "foreign forces," and fugitive "backflow"; says "a spark can start a fire" (星星之火可以燎原) ([HK01](https://www.hk01.com/article/60321528)).
- Sedition sentencing (Apr 14, 2026): **Raymond Chong Wai-man** (61), arrested by national-security police in November 2025, pleaded guilty at **West Kowloon Magistrates' Courts** to "knowingly publishing seditious publications" under the 2024 Safeguarding National Security Ordinance over **53 Facebook posts** (26 Mar 2024 – 29 Nov 2025) attacking the central and Hong Kong authorities. The posts ranged widely — Beijing's rule, Xi Jinping, calls for change — and **among them were comments on the Wang Fuk Court fire**: in one he suggested that if the fire sparked a resistance movement on the scale of the 2019 protests, Beijing "would not dare carry out a massacre like last time" (SCMP's rendering). The magistrate said the content "went beyond ordinary political expression" and openly challenged state power, noting the posts had drawn 654 likes, 90 comments and 47 shares; an 18-month starting point was cut to **12 months** for the guilty plea. His is among the first sentences handed down in the wave of fire-period sedition cases — a reminder that the "seditious publications" defendants flagged in the Feb 11 review (above) are ordinary residents prosecuted for social-media posts ([SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-and-crime/article/3350072/hong-kong-retiree-gets-one-year-jail-seditious-social-media-comments) · [法庭線 The Witness](https://thewitnesshk.com/61%E6%AD%B2%E7%94%B7%E8%AA%8D%E7%99%BC%E7%85%BD%E5%8B%95%E5%B8%96%E6%96%87%E5%88%A4%E5%9B%9A1%E5%B9%B4-%E5%AE%98%E6%8C%87%E5%85%A7%E5%AE%B9%E8%B6%85%E8%B6%8A%E4%B8%80%E8%88%AC%E6%94%BF%E6%B2%BB/) — court reporting preserved at [[法庭線|sites.thewitness]]).
- Commentator's trial opens (Oct 9, 2026): The trial of political commentator **Wong Kwok-ngon** (黃覺岸, pen name **Wong On-yin** / 王岸然) opened at the **District Court**, where he **pleaded not guilty** — representing himself — to both charges: "impeding a national-security investigation" (the **first prosecution** under the 2025 Article 88 offence) and "knowingly publishing seditious publications" (YouTube videos posted Jan 3–Dec 6, 2025, several about the Wang Fuk Court fire). In its opening the prosecution said that after the fire the national-security department received intelligence that Wong and others planned a press conference, and that officers had asked him to keep their meeting confidential; an NSD sergeant testified the intelligence indicated an attempt to "create social conflict" (製造社會矛盾) via a fire press conference. Eight hearing days are reserved and both offences carry up to **7 years** ([法庭線 The Witness](https://thewitnesshk.com/%E7%8E%8B%E5%B2%B8%E7%84%B6%E5%90%A6%E8%AA%8D%E5%A6%A8%E5%AE%B3%E8%AA%BF%E6%9F%A5%E5%8F%8A%E7%85%BD%E5%8B%95-%E5%9C%8B%E5%AE%89%E8%99%95%E8%AD%A6%E9%95%B7%E6%83%85%E5%A0%B1%E6%8C%87%E4%BC%81%E5%9C%96/) · [明報](https://news.mingpao.com/ins/%E6%B8%AF%E8%81%9E/article/20261009/s00001/1791528710639/%E7%8E%8B%E5%B2%B8%E7%84%B6%E6%B6%89%E5%A6%A8%E5%AE%B3%E5%9C%8B%E5%AE%89%E8%AA%BF%E6%9F%A5%E5%8F%8A%E7%99%BC%E7%85%BD%E5%8B%95%E5%BD%B1%E7%89%87-%E6%8E%A7%E6%96%B9%E6%8C%87%E8%A2%AB%E5%91%8A%E8%88%87%E5%9C%8B%E5%AE%89%E8%99%95%E6%9C%83%E9%9D%A2%E5%BE%8C%E7%99%BC%E7%89%87%E6%8A%AB%E9%9C%B2%E5%85%A7%E5%AE%B9) · court reporting preserved at [[法庭線|sites.thewitness]]).
- Commentator's trial — prosecution rests, case to answer (Oct 20, 2026): On the **seventh day** of the trial, the prosecution **closed its case** after playing the remaining videos, and District Judge dismissed the no-case submission, ruling there was a **prima facie case** (表證成立) on both charges; **Wong Kwok-ngon**, who is **representing himself**, was told to decide by **21 October** whether to give evidence or call witnesses. His main defences: that his meeting with national-security officers was **already widely reported** before he spoke of it, so he could not have "disclosed" something "everyone already knew" (「賣晒報紙」), and that the prosecution **never explained why his videos were seditious** rather than ordinary criticism. The prosecution maintained that his disclosure "tipped off" others and impeded the probe, and that the videos went beyond criticism or opinion; an NSD sergeant had testified that intelligence indicated a plan to "create social conflict" (製造社會矛盾) via a fire press conference. The case remains the **first prosecution** under the 2024 Ordinance's Article 88 ([法庭線 The Witness, Day 7](https://thewitnesshk.com/%E7%8E%8B%E5%B2%B8%E7%84%B6%E6%A1%88day7-%E7%8E%8B%E8%B3%AA%E7%96%91%E5%9C%8B%E5%AE%89%E7%B4%84%E8%AB%87%E7%9C%BE%E6%89%80%E5%91%A8%E7%9F%A5-%E4%B8%8D%E5%B1%AC%E6%8A%AB%E9%9C%B2%E8%AA%BF%E6%9F%A5/) · [SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-and-crime/article/3370378/news-commentator-denies-unlawfully-revealing-police-meeting-details-online)).
- **The homeowners'-meeting fight**: owners spent months trying to force a statutory general meeting with the government-appointed administrator **Hop On Management** (a Chinachem subsidiary). Their petition was referred to police over alleged forged signatures, the administrator tried to stall, and the Lands Tribunal refused the delay. The full sequence — petition, forgery referral, the Tribunal ruling and the first meeting on 19 July — is on [[hong-kong-fire-2025.resettlement]].

## Narrative and Information Control

*For the broader crackdown on Hong Kong's press and the outlets that covered this fire, see [[press-freedom]].*

- “One fire, two systems” framing: ABC analysis says grief and demands for accountability are colliding with Beijing’s red lines—petition organizer arrested, volunteers/NGOs ordered off-site, and residents’ safety complaints rebuffed; argues sovereignty-first governance erodes trust and turns routine civic action into political risk ([ABC EN](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-12-02/tai-po-fire-hong-kong-mainland-grief-red-lines/106087732) / [ABC 中](https://www.abc.net.au/chinese/2025-12-02/tai-po-fire-hong-kong-mainland-grief-red-lines/106092864)).
- Narrative contest on blame: Nikkei Asia op-ed argues officials’ focus on “bamboo scaffolding” is a diversion from systemic negligence—flammable foam/mesh, alarms that failed despite inspections, opaque site logs, and tender/bid-rigging risks. Notes contractor Prestige Construction & Engineering Ltd. (宏業建築工程有限公司) had prior safety offences and topped consultancy scores despite red flags, cites parallels to the 2010 Shanghai facade fire, and warns shrinking media/legislative oversight lets authorities recast a man-made disaster as accident ([Nikkei Asia](https://asia.nikkei.com/opinion/the-fire-that-hong-kong-wants-you-to-forget)).
- National security posture: Beijing’s national-security office warned it would punish anyone “exploiting” the fire for political ends, accused “anti-China” actors of spreading false information, and threatened arrests of those directing anger at the government. A person distributing fliers for an independent inquiry was detained and later bailed ([WSJ](https://www.wsj.com/world/china/hong-kongs-response-to-deadly-fire-is-squeezed-by-chinas-firm-hand-ea01b5a2)).
- Media summons (Dec 6): OSNS summoned senior journalists from outlets including AFP for a “regulatory talk,” claiming foreign media spread false info and smeared relief efforts/elections; officials read a statement, cited no specific stories, took no questions, and warned not to cross “red lines” with the phrase “don’t say we didn’t warn you” ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2025/12/06/dont-say-we-didnt-warn-you-chinas-nat-sec-office-in-hong-kong-summons-international-media/)).
- Government rebuttal to media: Security Secretary Chris Tang sent a letter to the Wall Street Journal criticizing its editorial on the fire as biased and “ignoring” government support measures, insisting law enforcement must act on alleged crimes and warning against “using the tragedy” (Now News, [letter coverage](https://news.now.com/home/local/player?newsId=628411)).
- Campus clampdown update: After earlier poster removals, Hong Kong Baptist University ordered its Students’ Union to suspend operations on Dec 5, citing low representativeness, welfare gaps, and finance-rule issues; it took over the SU office, copy room, and notice boards, giving officers <48 hours to clear belongings. HKBU SU condemned the move as unilateral and baseless and said it had already been revising finance rules and planning student events ([HKBU SU statement](https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1A5Q9xMkQ4/?mibextid=wwXIfr)).
- Disappearances/online takedowns: Threads/X accounts of Hailey Cheng (a.k.a. 金冬菇, founder of the GitHub “Hong Kong Fire Documentary” project) were removed early Dec 3; her phone unreachable, prompting fears she was taken for questioning over “seditious” information ([Threads](https://www.threads.com/@bravedogdog/post/DRxuZY8DOEH?xmt=AQF0lSY3idOhbSWh9l93EEyPuDBCKVB3sWO-7wYF0_7GxA)).
- Self-censorship after warnings: After Dec 3 OSNS/HKSAR statements about “foreign forces,” content creators Ellie Yuen (whose explainer amassed ~5.5M views) and Hailey Cheng said on Dec 4 they would stop covering the fire and asked media not to quote them, citing “obvious reasons” and pledges to comply with government appeals ([The Diplomat](https://thediplomat.com/2025/12/hong-kongs-grenfell-tower-moment-when-grief-became-sedition/)).
- Narrative contest: Global Voices op-ed (Dec 2) says the fire was man-made—rooted in MBIS tender/oversight failures and ignored complaints—and urges an independent inquiry; criticizes scapegoating bamboo and notes student arrest over a petition and pulled Ta Kung Pao bid-rigging reports as evidence of suppression ([Global Voices](https://globalvoices.org/2025/12/02/critics-say-hong-kong-fire-was-due-to-negligence-not-scaffolding/)).
- International media framing: AP (Dec 2) describes a “tip of an iceberg,” highlighting 7 of 20 net samples failing, alleged cost-cutting net swaps, alarms not sounding, suspension of 28 other projects, and national-security arrests of petition organizers amid concerns of systemic bid-rigging and weak oversight ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/hong-wang-china-dissent-fire-construction-ff953aec2bc0201b0e3255805a241fc1)).
- Freedoms and suppression: Foreign Policy column argues the fire confirms Hong Kong’s political culture now mirrors the mainland—civil society aid dismantled, petitioners arrested, independent inquiries impossible under NSL—contrasting Grenfell’s scrutiny with Hong Kong’s repression and warning disasters risk being buried in official narratives ([Foreign Policy](https://foreignpolicy.com/2025/12/02/hong-kong-apartment-fire-china-political-freedoms/)).
- UN concern over civic space: UN rights chief Volker Türk says “draconian” security laws are being used on people calling for an independent inquiry and better oversight after the fire; urges dropping those cases and warns cumulative NSL/Safeguarding Ordinance impacts are eroding expression, assembly, and association ([UN News](https://news.un.org/en/story/2025/12/1166548)).
- Missing voices and bamboo scapegoating: Taiwanese outlet Tian Jian reports locals fear bamboo-blame narratives distract from oversight failures and bid-rigging; notes ReNews’ multilingual corrections, PolyU’s Xinyan Huang apologizing for misstatements, Dec 6 Taipei vigil, and rising risk for Hong Kongers speaking to foreign media amid sedition arrests ([Tian Jian](https://tian-jian.org/hong-kong-tai-po-wang-fuk-court-fire/)).
- Parallel accountability push: HK01 opinion says “ironclad” evidence shows departmental failures (flammable foam sealing windows, fake net certificates, disabled alarms, altered smoke doors) and urges immediate internal probes/discipline at Housing Department, Labour Department, FSD, and Buildings Department instead of waiting for the judge-led committee ([HK01](https://www.hk01.com/01%E8%A7%80%E9%BB%9E/60302560/%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E5%A4%A7%E7%81%AB-%E8%A7%80%E9%BB%9E-%E5%A4%B1%E8%81%B7%E9%90%B5%E8%AD%89%E5%A6%82%E5%B1%B1-%E5%8F%8A%E6%97%A9%E8%BF%BD%E8%B2%AC%E8%A3%9C%E6%BC%8F)).
- Cultural defense of bamboo (Dec 5): Artists, architects, and cultural historians circulated multilingual explainers and posts like photographer Elaine Li’s “Leave the bamboo alone,” framing bamboo scaffolding as an intangible cultural symbol (akin to neon signs) and warning against scapegoating the craft after officials ordered scaffold mesh removals citywide ([Artnet](https://news.artnet.com/art-world/hong-kong-fire-bamboo-culture-2723917)).

## Donations and Aid
- Relief funds (as of Dec 2): Government-led assistance fund totals ~HK$2.3B (HK$2B donations + HK$300m seed); disbursements include HK$200k condolence and HK$50k funeral per fatality, plus HK$50k living allowance per affected household. As of latest: 21 condolence cases and 104 living-allowance cases processed (Now News).
- Philanthropy/property (Ming Pao, Dec 2): Li Ka Shing Foundation HK$80m (HK$30m immediate + HK$50m follow-on); Lee Shau Kee Foundation HK$30m; Lee Kum Kee charity HK$30m; Chow Tai Fook HK$20m; Sun Hung Kai Properties HK$20m + 160 hotel rooms; Sino Group + Wong Ting-fong Fund HK$20m + 160 hotel rooms; Wharf HK$30m; Hang Lung HK$11m + 20 Kornhill Apartments units for two months; Swire/Cathay/Swire Properties/Coca-Cola >HK$10m aid package ([Ming Pao](https://finance.mingpao.com/fin/instantf/20251202/1764214289065/%E5%A4%A7%E5%9F%94%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E4%BA%94%E7%B4%9A%E7%81%AB-%E6%9D%8E%E5%98%89%E8%AA%A0%E5%9F%BA%E9%87%91%E6%9C%83%E5%8C%AF%E8%B1%90%E4%B8%AD%E9%8A%80%E7%AD%89%E5%A4%9A%E9%96%93%E4%BC%81%E6%A5%AD%E6%8D%90%E6%AC%BE%E6%94%AF%E6%8F%B4%E3%80%90%E4%B8%8D%E6%96%B7%E6%9B%B4%E6%96%B0%E3%80%91#goog_rewarded)).
- Finance/insurance/tech/logistics (Ming Pao, Dec 2): HSBC + Hang Seng HK$30m; BOCHK HK$20m plus public donation account; Standard Chartered HK$10m; AIA total HK$40m; Prudential HK$20m; Manulife HK$20m; Sun Life HK$10m; FWD HK$10m plus HK$10k per affected policyholder; Tencent total HK$30m; Alibaba HK$20m; JD.com >RMB30m supplies; MTR HK$10m plus 2,000 Octopus cards preloaded HK$2,000 each; Disney >HK$10m cash/aid package ([Ming Pao](https://finance.mingpao.com/fin/instantf/20251202/1764214289065/%E5%A4%A7%E5%9F%94%E5%AE%8F%E7%A6%8F%E8%8B%91%E4%BA%94%E7%B4%9A%E7%81%AB-%E6%9D%8E%E5%98%89%E8%AA%A0%E5%9F%BA%E9%87%91%E6%9C%83%E5%8C%AF%E8%B1%90%E4%B8%AD%E9%8A%80%E7%AD%89%E5%A4%9A%E9%96%93%E4%BC%81%E6%A5%AD%E6%8D%90%E6%AC%BE%E6%94%AF%E6%8F%B4%E3%80%90%E4%B8%8D%E6%96%B7%E6%9B%B4%E6%96%B0%E3%80%91#goog_rewarded)).
- Tech: Apple says it is donating (amount undisclosed) to relief efforts for the Hong Kong fire and to storm/flood recovery across Thailand/Indonesia/Malaysia/Sri Lanka; Tim Cook posted condolences for the Hong Kong blaze and announced donations on Nov 25 and Dec 2 (MacRumors citing X posts [1](https://x.com/tim_cook/status/1994319685089702129) [2](https://x.com/tim_cook/status/1995900164519985451) [MacRumors](https://www.macrumors.com/2025/12/02/apple-donating-to-relief-efforts-in-asia/)).
- Retail/e-commerce: HKTVmall confirms HK$10m cash fully disbursed to the government “Wang Fuk Court Assistance Fund,” Po Leung Kuk, Tung Wah Group of Hospitals, and Yan Chai Hospital for financial/medical/lodging/reconstruction support; pledges continued supplies (bedding, small appliances, daily goods) and volunteer help ([eDigest](https://www.edigest.hk/news/hktvmall-%e8%b3%91%e7%81%bd%e6%8d%90%e6%ac%be-%e5%b7%b2%e5%88%b0%e4%bd%8d-1000%e8%90%ac%e7%8f%be%e9%87%91-%e7%8e%8b%e7%b6%ad%e5%9f%ba-%e5%8d%b3%e6%99%82%e8%b2%a1%e7%b6%93-1968587/4/)).
- Arts/crypto relief (Dec 5): Tron/HTX founder Justin Sun pledged HK$10m to the government relief fund; artist Ding Shilun and Bernheim Gallery staged a silent auction for St. John Ambulance Hong Kong; Artnet says additional art firms helped anonymously. Illustrator and resident Apple Tong lost supplies in the blaze and reported community donations after sharing her story ([Artnet](https://news.artnet.com/art-world/hong-kong-fire-bamboo-culture-2723917)).
- Donations tracker: the community-run **"Taipo Big Donations Watcher"** logged **HK$2.8276b** in pledges across **328 donors** ([GitHub](https://github.com/immartian/Taipo-Big-Donations-Watcher.github.io)).

## Community Support
- Volunteer logistics: ad hoc transport, food, and shelter assistance noted around Tai Po; emergency shelters and transitional housing placements ongoing.
- Foreign domestic workers: special arrangements coordinated with Indonesian and Philippine consulates; as of Dec 3, ten FDWs (9 Indonesian, 1 Filipino) confirmed dead and five injured, with broader unaccounted counts still being reconciled (UDN/TVBS/HKFP).
- Faith-based response (Dec 3): Christianity Today reports Tai Po Baptist Church sheltered residents and supported >60 displaced congregants, with pastors providing on-site counseling and praying during services; HKCNP coordinated pastors via Zoom and placed Hung Fook Tong donation boxes to aid rebuilding ([Christianity Today](https://www.christianitytoday.com/2025/12/hong-kong-apartments-fire-church-christians/)).

## Documentation
- Social Media Post Backup: community-collected archive of posts related to the fire and response ([Drive folder](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1OUFrVCpzJwofcBJeOTvv_9FDwI9yRzbe)).

1.v:
Related: [[⚖️ Jimmy Lai|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]] | [[Hong Kong Alliance|sites.hka]] | [[🎵 Glory to Hong Kong|glory-to-hong-kong]] | [[📕 Book Censorship under the NSL|book-censorship]]

The **Hong Kong 47** (民主派初選案) is the largest single prosecution ever brought under the 2020 **National Security Law** — a case that put nearly the entire front rank of the city's opposition in the dock at once. In the winter of 2021, **47 pro-democracy figures** — former lawmakers, district councillors, unionists, a journalist, students and academics — were charged with **conspiracy to commit subversion** for organising or standing in an **unofficial primary election**. Their alleged crime was to have tried to win a majority in the Legislative Council through the ballot box. By the time the courts were done, **45 of the 47 had been convicted** and jailed for terms of up to **10 years**, in a trial held **without a jury** before judges hand-picked for national-security cases.

## The "35+" plan

In July 2020, weeks after the NSL took effect, the pro-democracy camp held a **primary election** to pick a united slate for that autumn's Legislative Council poll. Despite official warnings that it might breach the new law, **more than 600,000 Hong Kong voters** turned out over the weekend of **11–12 July 2020** to choose candidates.

The strategy behind it — dubbed **"35+"** — was authored by legal scholar **Benny Tai Yiu-ting** (戴耀廷), a co-founder of the 2014 Occupy movement. The opposition had never held a majority in the partly-elected legislature; Tai argued that if democrats could win **35 or more** of the 70 seats, they could use the legislature's constitutional powers to **veto the government budget**. Under the Basic Law, a twice-rejected budget would force the Chief Executive either to dissolve the legislature or to **resign** — leverage the camp hoped to trade for the 2019 protest movement's "five demands," including universal suffrage.

Prosecutors cast this plan not as ordinary politics but as a plot to **paralyse the government** and "**overthrow**" the constitutional order. The trial judges agreed, describing the scheme as a "**constitutional mass destruction weapon**" aimed at toppling the Hong Kong government.

## The trial and verdict

The 47 were charged on **28 February 2021** and most were **denied bail**, held on remand for years before and during their trial. Of the 47, **31 pleaded guilty** and **16 pleaded not guilty**, contesting a case heard from early 2023 by **three designated national-security judges** rather than a jury.

On **30 May 2024**, the court **convicted 14** of the 16 who had fought the charge and **acquitted two** — barrister **Lawrence Lau Wai-chung** (勞偉聰) and district councillor **Lee Yue-shun** (李予信). Together with the 31 who pleaded guilty, **45 of the 47 stood convicted**. The Department of Justice, unhappy with the two acquittals, **appealed** them.

## The sentences (November 2024)

On **19 November 2024** the court handed down sentences ranging from **4 years 2 months to 10 years**, sorting the defendants into tiers by their role — "principal organisers," active participants, and others. Those who pleaded guilty received the customary one-third discount; four who **testified for the prosecution** (Au Nok-hin, Andrew Chiu, Ben Chung and Mike Lam) had their terms cut further.

| **Gwyneth Ho** 何桂藍 | Journalist-turned-candidate; gave no mitigation plea | **7 years** |
| **Au Nok-hin** 區諾軒 | Organiser; testified for the prosecution | 6 years 9 months |

In September 2026, **[[Joshua Wong|faces-of-the-crackdown.joshua-wong]]** — still in prison — **pleaded guilty to a separate national-security charge** of colluding with foreign forces, exposing him to further years behind bars beyond his primary-case term ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/01/china/hong-kong-joshua-wong-second-national-security-charge-intl-hnk)).

## The appeals

- **23 February 2026** — The **Court of Appeal rejected the appeals of all 12** activists who had challenged their convictions or sentences, endorsing the trial court's "constitutional mass destruction weapon" reasoning. In the same ruling it **dismissed the Department of Justice's appeal** against Lawrence Lau's acquittal, upholding his not-guilty verdict. Amnesty International called the decision "a missed opportunity to start restoring justice" ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/02/23/breaking-court-rejects-appeals-of-all-12-activists-in-landmark-hong-kong-47-national-security-case/) · [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/23/hong-kong-court-rejects-appeal-in-landmark-subversion-case) · [Amnesty](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/02/hong-kong-rejected-appeals-in-hk-47-case-a-missed-opportunity-to-start-restoring-justice/)).
- **10 August 2026** — The Court of Appeal granted **11 of the jailed democrats leave to appeal to the Court of Final Appeal**, the city's apex court — the **first time** the case's core national-security questions will be tested at that level. The three appellate judges, led by High Court Chief Judge **Jeremy Poon**, said the appeals "merit the consideration by the Court of Final Appeal." Among the eleven are **Gwyneth Ho** and **Leung Kwok-hung** ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/08/10/hong-kong-47-11-jailed-democrats-granted-permission-to-appeal-to-top-court/)).

By early 2026, some of the shorter-sentenced defendants — credited with years already spent on remand — had begun to be **released**, even as the longest-serving face years still to run and the final appeal remains pending.

## Why it matters

The case criminalised the ordinary machinery of opposition politics — a primary, a manifesto, a plan to win seats and use them. Prosecutors did not allege violence; the "subversion" lay in the **intention to win a legislative majority and use its budget veto**. That theory, now upheld on appeal, marks how far the NSL has redrawn the limits of dissent: the same years that saw the [[Hong Kong Alliance|sites.hka]] convicted for a Tiananmen slogan, [[faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]] jailed for his newspaper, and the city's [[bookshops raided|book-censorship]], also saw an entire pro-democracy generation — its scholars, students, unionists and reporters — imprisoned for contesting an election.

> "Glory to Hong Kong" is a march that was composed and written by a musician under the pseudonym "Thomas dgx yhl", with the contribution of a group of Hongkonger netizens from the online forum LIHKG during the 2019–2020 Hong Kong protests. It was initially written in Cantonese and was eventually developed into various language versions. It has been adopted as the anthem of these protests, with some considering it the "national anthem of Hong Kong". — Wikipedia

## Origin & Creation

"Glory to Hong Kong" (願榮光歸香港) emerged in August–September 2019 at the height of the anti-extradition-bill protests. The melody and initial lyrics were written by an anonymous composer using the handle **"Thomas dgx yhl"**, then refined collaboratively by users of the **LIHKG** forum — an unusually crowd-sourced act of authorship. The first orchestral/choral recording and music video were posted in September 2019 and spread rapidly; crowds soon sang it in shopping malls, on streets, and at protest rallies, where it functioned as a de facto anthem of the movement. Its closing line carries the 2019 slogan **"光復香港，時代革命"** ("Liberate Hong Kong, revolution of our times").

## Censorship & the Court Ban

As the most recognisable cultural artifact of the 2019 movement, the song became a primary target of the post-National-Security-Law crackdown — making it a fitting entry in this archive.

> ⚖️ **The legal case in depth:** the ban was a civil injunction, refused by the High Court in 2023 and granted by the Court of Appeal in 2024. The two judgments — the arguments on both sides, and the documents themselves — are preserved and set out on **[[The Court Ban — Judgments & Arguments|glory-to-hong-kong.injunction]]**.

- **2020–2022** — After the 2020 National Security Law, schools, broadcasters, and platforms come under pressure to suppress the song; singing or playing it is treated as potentially seditious.
- **Nov 2022 onward — sporting mix-ups**: At international events involving Hong Kong teams (e.g. the Asia Rugby Sevens in Incheon, South Korea, Nov 2022, and an ice-hockey championship in 2023), organisers mistakenly played "Glory to Hong Kong" instead of China's official anthem "March of the Volunteers." Officials blamed Google's search algorithm for surfacing the protest song at the top of results, and the government repeatedly demanded corrections.
- **June 2023** — The Department of Justice files for a **court injunction** to ban the song. Around the same time it is **pulled from major streaming platforms** (Spotify, Apple Music, KKBOX) after its distributor removes it — only to reappear in other versions.
- **July 2023** — The **Court of First Instance refuses** the injunction, citing free-expression concerns and a potential "chilling effect" on legitimate use.
- **8 May 2024** — The **Court of Appeal overturns** the lower court and **grants the injunction**, making "Glory to Hong Kong" the first song banned in Hong Kong since the 1997 handover. The order prohibits "broadcasting, performing, printing, publishing, selling, offering for sale, distributing, disseminating, displaying or reproducing" the song with **seditious intent**, to **advocate Hong Kong independence**, or to **suggest it is Hong Kong's national anthem** — while exempting lawful journalistic and academic activity ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2024/05/08/breaking-govt-bid-to-ban-glory-to-hong-kong-protest-song-approved-by-appeals-court/) · [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/5/8/hong-kong-court-bans-protest-song-glory-to-hong-kong)).
- **15 May 2024** — **YouTube blocks** access to dozens of video versions of the song for users in Hong Kong, complying with the court order; Google says it is "disappointed" ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2024/05/15/media/youtube-glory-to-hong-kong-intl-hnk)).
- **25 May & 7 June 2024** — Distributor **EmuBands removes** the song from Apple Music, Spotify, Facebook, and Instagram again following the court order ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2024/05/25/glory-to-hong-kong-distributor-removes-hong-kong-protest-song-from-spotify-apple-music-after-court-order/) · [HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2024/06/07/protest-song-glory-to-hong-kong-removed-from-streaming-platforms-again/)).

Despite removals, the song persists through mirrors, re-uploads, offline copies, and international performances — the precise pattern of dispersal-as-preservation this project documents.

## Prosecutions & Arrests

Even before the 2024 injunction, authorities prosecuted people for performing, sharing, or remixing the song — and, rather than relying on any direct ban, they reached for whatever offence fit: **sedition**, the **National Anthem Ordinance**, humble **busking-permit** rules, and, more recently, **inciting subversion** under the National Security Law. Documented cases:

- **Lai Rifu (賴日福) — Sept 2019, mainland China**: A Guangzhou activist was detained for "picking quarrels and provoking trouble" after sharing a video that used "Glory to Hong Kong" as background music — among the earliest known prosecutions tied to the song ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glory_to_Hong_Kong)).
- **Harmonica player at the Queen's vigil — Sept 19, 2022**: A 43-year-old man surnamed **Pang** was arrested on suspicion of sedition (colonial-era Crimes Ordinance) after playing the tune on a harmonica among mourners outside the British Consulate during Queen Elizabeth II's funeral; he was released on bail pending investigation ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2022/09/21/asia/hong-kong-harmonica-arrest-sedition-intl-hnk-mic/index.html)).
- **Rugby anthem-blunder video — Nov 2022**: A 49-year-old man was arrested for sedition over social-media posts praising and sharing footage of "Glory to Hong Kong" being played instead of China's anthem at an overseas rugby match (the Incheon Asia Rugby Sevens); he was denied bail and later convicted ([SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-and-crime/article/3203609/court-convicts-hong-kong-man-sedition-over-social-media-posts-including-footage-anthem-blunder)).
- **Chui Hoi-chun — Dec 2022 / appeal Dec 2025**: Sentenced in Dec 2022 to a training-centre order after pleading guilty to four offences, including sedition for publishing **altered lyrics** of the song and insulting the national anthem. On **Dec 18, 2025** the Court of Appeal allowed his sentence appeal and he **walked free**, having already spent more than two years on bail awaiting the hearing ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2025/12/19/hong-kong-man-convicted-on-sedition-insulting-national-anthem-charges-walks-free-after-winning-sentence-appeal/)).
- **Cheng Wing-chun (鄭永俊) — convicted Jul 2023**: A 27-year-old photographer became the **first person tried under the 2020 National Anthem Ordinance**, convicted on Jul 5 and jailed for **three months** on Jul 20, 2023 (plus a flag-desecration charge) for a YouTube clip that replaced "March of the Volunteers" with "Glory to Hong Kong" over footage of fencer Edgar Cheung winning Olympic gold at Tokyo 2020. Magistrate Minnie Wat said he "encouraged others to commit acts damaging to national dignity" ([RFA](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/hk-anthem-07202023160232.html)).
- **Li Jiexin (李解新), the "erhu uncle" (二胡伯伯) — jailed Oct 2023 & again Aug 2024**: A retired street musician, **69 at the time of his arrest**, was repeatedly prosecuted for playing "Glory to Hong Kong" on the **erhu** (二胡) at Tai Wai, Mong Kok and the Central IFC footbridge between Aug 2021 and Sep 2022. In his first trial he pleaded not guilty, cast the prosecution as "**political persecution**," and invoked free-expression protections under the **ICCPR** — the court hearing that the prosecution's reading of the UN treaty was "too narrow." On **Oct 25, 2023** he was convicted of seven counts of performing and fundraising without a permit and jailed **30 days**; the magistrate leaned on the government's injunction ruling that the song carries secessionist and seditious force (and its "光復香港，時代革命" refrain), branding his busking a form of "**soft resistance**" (軟對抗). He dropped his appeal and served the term at once. Charged again over further street performances, he **pleaded guilty to eight of twelve summonses** and on **Aug 7, 2024** was jailed **18 days** and had **two erhus confiscated** (Judge Ivy Chui, West Kowloon). Hong Kong Watch lists him as a political prisoner ([The Witness](https://thewitnesshk.com/%E8%A2%AB%E6%8C%87%E8%A1%97%E9%A0%AD%E4%BA%8C%E8%83%A1%E5%A5%8F%E9%A1%98%E6%A6%AE%E5%85%89-%E5%85%AD%E6%97%AC%E7%BF%81%E7%84%A1%E7%89%8C%E6%BC%94%E5%A5%8F%E7%AD%89%E7%BD%AA/) · [RFA Cantonese](https://www.rfa.org/cantonese/news/htm/hkcourt/hk-play-01262023062636.html) · [HKFP: 30 days](https://hongkongfp.com/2023/10/25/elderly-busker-who-played-protest-song-glory-to-hong-kong-sentenced-to-30-days-in-prison/) · [HKFP: 2nd jailing](https://hongkongfp.com/2024/08/07/elderly-busker-jailed-for-second-time-over-performing-protest-anthem-glory-to-hong-kong/) · [HKW](https://www.hongkongwatch.org/political-prisoner/2024/10/30/li-jie-xin)).
- **Chan Ho-hin — inciting subversion, 2025–26**: A 23-year-old **waiter** became an example of the banned anthem surfacing in a **national-security subversion** case rather than a sedition or anthem-law one. Between June 2024 and April 2025 he posted **1,184 messages on X** and put up A4 street posters in Yau Ma Tei and Wong Tai Sin promoting a pro-Taiwan "Revive the Republic of China" party; **seven of the posts featured "Glory to Hong Kong"** as the city's purported "regional anthem." Originally charged in April 2025 with publishing seditious material under the **Article 23 law**, the charge was **upgraded to inciting subversion** under the Beijing-imposed National Security Law; he pleaded guilty and was sentenced in **July 2026 to about two years four months** ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/07/10/hong-kong-waiter-pleads-guilty-to-inciting-subversion-via-online-posts-street-posters/) · [SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/law-and-crime/article/3359961/hong-kong-man-pleads-guilty-subversive-promotion-pro-taiwan-party)).

Parent: [[Glory to Hong Kong|glory-to-hong-kong]] The ban on "Glory to Hong Kong" was not a statute but a **civil injunction** — and it was won only on appeal, after the High Court had refused it. Because the two judgments turn on the same question (can a court use a sweeping civil order to enforce the criminal law protecting national security, and at what cost to free expression?) and reach opposite answers, they are among the most important free-expression documents of the post-2020 period. This page sets out the arguments on both sides and preserves the judgments themselves. ## What the government sought By a summons of **5 June 2023**, the **Secretary for Justice** (Benjamin Yu SC) applied under **section 21L(1) of the High Court Ordinance** for an **interlocutory injunction "in aid of the criminal law"** — expressly **contra mundum** ("against the world"), binding people not yet identified. It was **not** a complete ban: it targeted **four classes of act** involving the Song (and 32 specific URLs listed in a Schedule) — - done **with intent / in circumstances capable of inciting secession** (NSL 21) or with **seditious intention** (Crimes Ordinance s.9); - done so as to be **likely mistaken for, or suggested to be, Hong Kong's "national anthem,"** with intent to insult the national anthem (National Anthem Ordinance s.7); - and in particular to **advocate separating the HKSAR from the PRC** — while **exempting lawful academic and news/journalistic activity**. On 8 July 2023 the **Chief Executive issued a certificate under NSL 47** certifying that the four acts involve national security, which is **binding on the courts**. The government's real aim was disclosed in its own case: criminal prosecution alone had not stopped the Song spreading, and it wanted a court order it could hand to **internet platform operators**. **Google had refused** the HKSAR's requests (since November 2022) to remove videos — including ones mislabelled "Hong Kong National Anthem" — **without "a valid court order demonstrating the relevant contents' violation of Hong Kong law."** The injunction was designed to be that order. ## Round 1 — the High Court refuses (28 July 2023) **[2023] HKCFI 1950** (HCA 855/2023), **Anthony Chan J** — application **dismissed**. The defendants did not appear; **Abraham Chan SC and Martin Ho served as amici curiae**. The core reasoning: - **The test is necessity / utility.** An injunction in aid of the criminal law must be shown to restrain conduct that the criminal law cannot — it must provide *greater* deterrence than the existing offences and be enforceable. - **The criminal regime is already "extensive and robust."** The NSL, Crimes Ordinance and National Anthem Ordinance — with NSL enforcement overseen by a dedicated office and police unit — already cover these acts, some carrying **up to life imprisonment** (NSL). The judge was "**not satisfied that the Injunction is of any real utility**," and saw "a real risk that the Injunction would conflict with the criminal law regime in terms of enforcement." - **A matter of principle.** It "may seem wrong" for a *civil* court to grant an order whose breach carries open-ended contempt sanctions "to do what [the legislature] has not done," still less to "pass judgment on what is effectively a serious criminal offence, **without the procedural safeguards of the criminal justice system**." A newcomer who breached it would face **both contempt and criminal prosecution** for the same act. - **Third parties and "chilling effects."** Because the order ran against the whole of Hong Kong and would likely never go to trial, the court had to scrutinise it stringently to protect the rights of innocent third parties — "a whole spectrum of Hong Kong people of different sophistication," who might **"distance themselves from what may be lawful acts involving the Song for fear of trespassing the Injunction."** The injunction was "not an easy document to understand." - **No blanket deference.** The judge **declined to simply defer to the executive** on the *utility* question: "The Court cannot abdicate its responsibilities… [it] must scrutinize the material before it." (He accepted the executive is better placed to judge whether the acts *endanger* national security.) - On the **Hysan four-step proportionality test** he found a legitimate aim, but — "**but for**" the failures of utility and the conflict with the criminal law — would have granted it. Those qualifications were fatal: it was not "just and convenient" to grant. **Dismissed.** ## Round 2 — the Court of Appeal grants it (8 May 2024) **[2024] HKCA 442** (CACV 274/2023), before **Poon CJHC, Chu VP and Anthea Pang JA** (heard 19 Dec 2023 & 24 Feb 2024) — appeal **allowed**, the injunction **granted**. Benjamin Yu SC and **Jenkin Suen SC** for the Secretary; the same amici. The reversal rested on reframing the question around national security: - **These are not ordinary crimes.** What the injunction enjoins are **offences endangering national security** (NSL 21, Crimes Ordinance s.10, NAO s.7). That character "**critically informs how the court should approach the injunction sought**." - **The court's own NSL duty.** **NSL 3 and NSL 8** impose a duty on the HKSAR's institutions — the courts included — to safeguard national security and to enforce the law to that end. The Court held that the established common-law principles for injunctions in aid of the criminal law can and should be **"suitably developed to give effect to the mandates in the NSL."** (It rejected Mr Yu's most sweeping formulation — that utility alone should decide — but still moved the balance decisively toward granting.) - **Utility re-assessed.** Set against the national-security backdrop — the Song's use in 413+ public-order events, its misrepresentation as the "national anthem" 887 times including at international sporting events, and platforms' refusal to act without a court order — the Court found the injunction *would* add real value, and **disagreed** with the first judge's conclusions on utility and on conflict with the criminal law. - The order was granted **contra mundum**, keeping the **academic / news-activity carve-out**, listing the 32 items, and providing for substituted service via government websites and a QR-coded notice. ## The two courts, side by side Few cases make the stakes so plain: on the **same facts and the same law**, two courts reached **opposite conclusions** a year apart. What moved between them was not the evidence but how much weight national security was allowed to carry against rights-scrutiny. | The question | High Court — **refused** (2023)
Anthony Chan J | Court of Appeal — **granted** (2024)
Poon CJHC · Chu VP · Pang JA | | --- | --- | --- | | Real utility beyond the existing criminal law? | **No** — the NSL/Crimes/Anthem regime is already "extensive and robust" | **Yes** — read against the national-security backdrop | | A civil order (contempt) for a serious crime? | May be wrong in principle; lacks criminal procedural safeguards | The common-law principles can be "developed" to give effect to the NSL | | Weight of the executive's security assessment? | Court judges utility **for itself** — "cannot abdicate its responsibilities" | **NSL 3 & 8 duty** critically informs the s.21L exercise | | Chilling effect on innocent third parties? | **Real, and decisive** | Outweighed; the academic/news carve-out suffices | | **Outcome** | Not "just and convenient" → **refused** | Appeal allowed → **injunction granted** | ## Why it was controversial The acts the injunction targets were **already crimes**, so the dispute was never about whether inciting secession is protected expression — it is not. The controversy is about the **method**, and much of it was spelled out in the first judgment itself: - **A civil order doing criminal work.** The same conduct could now trigger **both** criminal prosecution **and** contempt of court — the latter decided on the civil standard, without a jury or the safeguards of a criminal trial. The High Court thought it "may seem wrong" for a civil court to use open-ended contempt sanctions "to do what [the legislature] has not done." - **Binding "the world" with no adversary.** A *contra mundum* order reaches people who are **unnamed, unrepresented, and never heard**, including future "newcomers"; the case was unlikely ever to reach trial, making a sweeping, effectively **permanent** prohibition that was created without anyone there to contest it. - **The chilling effect the two courts split on.** The government argued the order "only bans crimes" and so cannot chill lawful speech; the High Court disagreed, finding ordinary people would avoid lawful uses of the Song "for fear of trespassing the Injunction," which is "not an easy document to understand." That the order needed a **carve-out for journalism and academia** concedes the risk was real — and the Court of Appeal then granted the very order the first court said would chill expression. - **Deference to the executive on national security.** Because **NSL 3 and 8** make safeguarding national security a duty of the courts, and the Chief Executive's **NSL 47 certificate binds** them on whether the acts endanger it, the room for independent proportionality scrutiny narrows. Free-expression scholars read the reversal as national-security **deference shading into domination** ([Columbia Global Freedom of Expression](https://globalfreedomofexpression.columbia.edu/cases/case-of-glory-to-hong-kong-song); [PEN America](https://pen.org/re-hong-kong-injunction-seeking-to-ban-glory-to-hong-kong/)). - **Censorship routed through private platforms.** The order's real function was to be the "valid court order" **Google** had said it required before removing videos; YouTube then **geo-blocked** the 32 listed videos in Hong Kong. A local court order thereby reshaped a global platform's feed — a template other governments could follow. Underlying all of it is a tension **internal to the record**: an injunction "in aid of the criminal law" is justified only where it is genuinely *necessary*, yet the Song remains freely available worldwide — so the order's value looks largely **expressive** (marking the Song as forbidden) rather than effective, which is precisely the "utility" the first court found wanting. ## Weighed against free-expression rights Hong Kong's free-expression guarantees are not merely domestic. **Article 27** of the Basic Law protects freedom of speech, of the press and of publication, and **Article 39** keeps the **International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR)** in force as applied to Hong Kong, implemented through the **Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance** (BOR Article 16 mirrors **ICCPR Article 19**). Under ICCPR 19(3), a restriction on expression is permissible only if it passes a **three-part test**: it must be (1) **provided by law** — precise enough to foresee what is forbidden; (2) in pursuit of a **legitimate aim** (national security is one); and (3) genuinely **necessary and proportionate** — the *least restrictive means* of achieving that aim. Measured against that standard, the injunction attracts several serious objections: - **Legal certainty (the "provided by law" limb).** The prohibition turns on the actor's *intent* ("with seditious intention," "capable of inciting") and on others' *perceptions* ("likely to be mistaken as the national anthem"), and extends to "any adaptation… substantially the same." A person cannot foresee with precision where lawful use ends and contempt begins — the very defect the High Court flagged when it called the order "not an easy document to understand," amid a wave of inaccurate reports that "the song is banned." International human-rights law treats such vague speech restrictions as failing the legality requirement, because they chill protected expression. - **Overbreadth and prior restraint.** A *contra mundum* ban on an entire cultural work — melody, lyrics and adaptations — reaches far beyond the unlawful acts it names, sweeping in artistic, educational, commemorative, scholarly, archival and private uses that are protected expression. International standards treat blanket prior restraints on a *category* of expression as presumptively suspect and demand the narrowest possible tailoring; the carve-out the court had to add for journalism and academia is itself an admission that protected speech was caught. - **Necessity.** ICCPR 19(3) requires a *real* need and the least restrictive means, not a symbolic one. The first court found the injunction added nothing the criminal law did not already do — which is the definition of *not necessary*. A measure that merely duplicates existing offences imposes an extra burden on expression without the countervailing necessity the Covenant requires. - **National security must narrow, not widen, the restriction.** The UN Human Rights Committee's **General Comment No. 34** on Article 19 holds that national security may *never* be invoked to suppress legitimate expression, and that a state must demonstrate a **direct and immediate connection** between the expression and a concrete threat, by proportionate means; the 1995 **Johannesburg Principles** on national security and free expression say the same. The Court of Appeal's reasoning runs the other way — treating the courts' NSL duty as a reason to *relax* the scrutiny that is supposed to constrain the aim, which is the structure these standards warn against. - **The audience's right, and censorship by proxy.** Article 19(2) protects the right to *seek and receive* information and ideas, not only to speak. Engineering a court order so that **Google and YouTube** would geo-block content turns private intermediaries into instruments of state censorship and restricts the public's access as much as any speaker's — a structural danger identified in UN Special Rapporteur reporting on freedom of expression online and in the **Manila Principles on Intermediary Liability**. - **Peaceful political and artistic expression.** Much use of the Song is peaceful political or artistic expression — the speech Article 19 protects most strongly, even when it criticises the authorities or voices views the state rejects. International law permits restricting only incitement to imminent violence or concrete unlawful acts, and narrowly; a blanket ban that reaches peaceful performance, mourning and art overshoots that line. To its critics, then, the injunction is close to a textbook failure of the three-part test: **uncertain in scope, broader than necessary, duplicative of the criminal law already in force, and justified by a national-security logic that the governing human-rights standards say should tighten restrictions on speech, not loosen the scrutiny of them.** The Hong Kong courts applied the local four-step proportionality test in [Hysan Development Co Ltd v Town Planning Board](https://www.hklii.hk/en/cases/hkcfa/2016/66) and divided on the result; measured against the ICCPR standard the Basic Law incorporates, the first judgment's refusal is the one that most critics regard as the better fit with the right. (See also [Columbia Global Freedom of Expression](https://globalfreedomofexpression.columbia.edu/cases/case-of-glory-to-hong-kong-song) and [PEN America](https://pen.org/re-hong-kong-injunction-seeking-to-ban-glory-to-hong-kong/).) ## Why it matters "Glory to Hong Kong" became the **first song banned in Hong Kong since the 1997 handover**, and the case is now studied as a turning point in how the city's courts weigh the National Security Law against protected rights (above). In practice the injunction did what the government wanted: Google **geo-blocked the 32 listed videos** in Hong Kong, and the distributor **EmuBands** again pulled the Song from Spotify, Apple Music and other platforms. Yet the melody is still everywhere — sung in the diaspora, mislabelled at sporting events, adapted and re-uploaded — a reminder that a court order can mark a song as contraband without erasing it. ## Preserved documents The archive keeps its own copies of both judgments (official Judiciary text), in case the public sources change: | Judgment | Our copy | Official | | --- | --- | --- | | **CFI — injunction refused** ([2023] HKCFI 1950, 28 Jul 2023) | [PDF](https://pub-24ab8cd7de4a4b2fa258f19bdf31e115.r2.dev/legal/glory-to-hong-kong/HKCFI_2023_1950_Glory-to-HK_CFI-refusal.pdf) | [HKLII](https://www.hklii.hk/en/cases/hkcfi/2023/1950) · [Judiciary (Word)](https://legalref.judiciary.hk/doc/judg/word/vetted/other/en/2023/HCA000855_2023.docx) | | **CA — injunction granted** ([2024] HKCA 442, 8 May 2024) | [PDF](https://pub-24ab8cd7de4a4b2fa258f19bdf31e115.r2.dev/legal/glory-to-hong-kong/HKCA_2024_442_Glory-to-HK_CA-grant.pdf) | [HKLII](https://www.hklii.hk/en/cases/hkca/2024/442) · [Judiciary (Word)](https://legalref.judiciary.hk/doc/judg/word/vetted/other/en/2023/CACV000274_2023.docx) | ## Sources - Some of the fullest records of Hong Kong's decade of dissent are not documents but **films** — shot on the front lines of 2019, dramatised from its memories, or imagined a decade ahead. Many of them can no longer be shown in the city they portray. A **2021 amendment to the Film Censorship Ordinance** empowered censors to **ban any film "contrary to the interests of national security,"** and to revoke the approval of films already passed — the moving-image counterpart to the [[criminalisation of books|book-censorship]]. The result is a body of work preserved and screened everywhere except home. This page gathers it, with each film's trailer and, where possible, where it can still be seen.

> A note on the clips below: these are the films' **official trailers** (and, for *Do Not Split*, the full film) as published by their makers and distributors. Where a film was released free by its creators, we point to that; otherwise we link where it can be bought or streamed.

## Ten Years (十年, 2015) — the warning

Where this story arguably begins. **_Ten Years_** is a **speculative anthology** of five short films — by directors **Ng Ka-leung, Jevons Au, Chow Kwun-wai, Kwok Zune and Wong Fei-pang** — imagining Hong Kong in **2025**: Mandarin displacing Cantonese, youth "guards" policing bookshops, a self-immolation outside the British consulate. Made for about HK$500,000, it became a surprise hit — outdrawing *Star Wars* at one Yau Ma Tei cinema — and won **Best Film at the 35th Hong Kong Film Awards (2016)**. Beijing's response was a preview of what came later: mainland outlets were ordered to condemn or ignore it, and **state television did not broadcast the awards ceremony** for the first time in decades. Its cinema run was quietly curtailed at home. Ten years on, much of what it imagined has arrived. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt5269560/))

## The 2019 uprising on film

### Cockroach (2020)

Dissident artist **Ai Weiwei**'s **93-minute** documentary — its title the slur ("**曱甴**", *gaat zaat*, cockroach) that police and pro-Beijing media hurled at protesters, reclaimed — assembles front-line footage of the 2019 movement from its peaceful marches to the **siege of Polytechnic University**. Directed by Ai from exile in Europe using material gathered on the ground, it was released internationally on video-on-demand (**Vimeo**, MUBI, Alamo) in December 2020 and, like the others here, has had no Hong Kong release. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt13696108/) · [Vimeo On Demand](https://vimeo.com/ondemand/cockroach))

### Do Not Split (2020)

Norwegian director **Anders Hammer**'s **35-minute** front-line short for **Field of Vision** — teargas, water cannon, the siege months — earned a **2021 Academy Award nomination** for Best Documentary Short. The nomination alone was enough for Beijing to **order mainland broadcasters not to carry the Oscars live**. Field of Vision released the film **free online**, so it remains one of the most-watched records of 2019. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt11512676/))

### Inside the Red Brick Wall (理大圍城, 2020)

An **88-minute** account of the **November 2019 siege of Hong Kong Polytechnic University**, shot from inside the campus by an anonymous collective calling itself **Hong Kong Documentary Filmmakers** (with a companion film, **_Taking Back the Legislature_**, on the 1 July 2019 storming of the legislature). Distributed by **Ying e Chi**, its Hong Kong screenings were cancelled and disrupted in 2020, and after the 2021 censorship amendment it became effectively unshowable in the city; it circulates through international festivals and distributors instead. It won Best Editing at **IDFA**. (IMDb: [Inside the Red Brick Wall](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt14266320/) · [Taking Back the Legislature](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt13236520/))

### Revolution of Our Times (時代革命, 2021)

Director **Kiwi Chow**'s **152-minute** chronicle of the movement — the marquee protest documentary. It was slipped into the **2021 Cannes** line-up as a last-minute, unannounced world premiere to avoid a diplomatic reaction, and won **Best Documentary at Taiwan's Golden Horse Awards**. To protect himself, Chow **sold the rights abroad and destroyed his own footage**; the film has **never been shown in Hong Kong** and its title — the 2019 protest slogan — is itself now treated as seditious. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt15049118/))

### Blue Island (憂鬱之島, 2022)

**Chan Tze-woon**'s **97-minute hybrid** documentary has protesters of 2019 re-enact the flights and imprisonments of an earlier generation — 1967 leftists, Cultural Revolution swimmers, the 1989 exiles — braiding decades of Hong Kong upheaval together. It won **Best Feature Documentary at Hot Docs 2022** and screens internationally rather than at home. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt15282802/))

### Faceless (2021)

Journalist **Jennifer Ngo**'s debut follows four anonymous participants — "the Student," "the Artist," "the Believer," "the Daughter" — through the anti-extradition movement, the masks a reminder of the cost of being seen. Distributed by **Dogwoof**. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt14489394/))

### May You Stay Forever Young (少年, 2021)

Not a documentary but a **dramatisation** — directors **Rex Ren** and **Lam Sum** restage a real effort by protesters, volunteers and a social worker to find and stop a teenager from taking her own life during the 2019 unrest. Denied release in Hong Kong, it premiered at **Golden Horse**, where it won the NETPAC award. ([IMDb](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt15743130/))

Behind Hong Kong's national-security statistics are people. By mid-2026, more than **410 people had been arrested** on national-security grounds since the law took effect in June 2020, over **210 charged** and **180-plus convicted or awaiting sentence** — the publishers, students, unionists, lawmakers, journalists and clergy who made up the city's civil society. Some are serving long prison terms; others fled into exile with bounties on their heads; a few were tried and cleared. This page gathers them — a human index to the crackdown documented across this archive, linking the individuals and cases we have profiled in depth.

## The press

The clearest target was Hong Kong's free media (see [[Book Censorship under the NSL|book-censorship]] for the printed word).

- **[[Jimmy Lai|faces-of-the-crackdown.jimmy-lai]]** (黎智英) — founder of *Apple Daily*; sentenced to **20 years** for foreign collusion and sedition, the harshest NSL term to date. Six *Apple Daily* executives were jailed for 6 years 9 months to 10 years.
- **Chung Pui-kuen** (鍾沛權) & **Patrick Lam** (林紹桐) — editors of *Stand News*, convicted in the first **sedition** case against a Hong Kong media outlet since the handover; Chung was jailed for **21 months**.

## The Hong Kong 47

The largest NSL case — 45 democrats jailed for organising a 2020 opposition primary. Full account and the sentence table on the **[[The Hong Kong 47|hong-kong-47]]** page. Among them:

- **Benny Tai** (戴耀廷) — legal scholar and "mastermind" of the plan: **10 years**, the longest.
- **[[Joshua Wong|faces-of-the-crackdown.joshua-wong]]** (黃之鋒) — face of the 2014 Umbrella Movement: **4 years 8 months**, and in 2026 he pleaded guilty to a **second** collusion charge carrying up to life.
- **Gwyneth Ho** (何桂藍, journalist, 7 years), **Owen Chow** (鄒家成, 7 years 9 months), **Gordon Ng** (吳政亨, 7 years 3 months), **Leung Kwok-hung** "Long Hair" (梁國雄, 6 years 9 months), **Winnie Yu** (余慧明, unionist, 6 years 9 months) and dozens more.

## The Tiananmen vigil and the Alliance

The leaders who kept the [[Tiananmen Vigil|tiananmen-vigil]] alive for thirty years, convicted in 2026 of inciting subversion (see [[Hong Kong Alliance|sites.hka]]):

- **[[Chow Hang-tung|faces-of-the-crackdown.chow-hang-tung]]** (鄒幸彤) — barrister and vigil convenor: **7 years 3 months**.
- **Lee Cheuk-yan** (李卓人) — Alliance chair and veteran unionist: **7 years**.
- **Albert Ho** (何俊仁) — founding member and former lawmaker: **5 years 2 months**.

## Faith

- **Cardinal Joseph Zen** (陳日君) — the 90-something retired Catholic bishop of Hong Kong and a trustee of the [[612 Humanitarian Relief Fund|sites.612fund]], **arrested in 2022** under the NSL and convicted of failing to register the fund; fined but not jailed — a signal that not even the Church was beyond reach.

## Driven abroad

Others escaped Hong Kong before they could be jailed, only to be declared fugitives and stripped of their passports. Since July 2023, **34 people living abroad** have been named in national-security arrest warrants with police rewards attached, and their families in Hong Kong have been questioned and, in one case, jailed. The full record, with who they are, what they do and what has been done to their families, is at **[[🌏 Pursued Abroad|pursued-abroad]]**.

- **Nathan Law** (羅冠聰, UK), **Agnes Chow** (周庭, Canada), [[Joshua Wong|faces-of-the-crackdown.joshua-wong]]'s Demosistō co-founders. Chow is wanted "for life" over bail, though without a reward.
- **Ted Hui** (許智峯, Australia), **Dennis Kwok** (郭榮鏗), **Kevin Yam** (任建峰), **Anna Kwok** (郭鳳儀), **Finn Lau** (劉祖廸), **Simon Cheng** (鄭文傑), **Frances Hui** (許穎婷), **Carmen Lau** (劉珈汶), **Chloe Cheung** (張晞晴) and others named on successive lists, pursued for lobbying, testimony, journalism or organising abroad.

## Help complete this record

This is a living index, and it is far from complete — hundreds more remain unnamed here. If you can help profile someone, correct a detail, or contribute photographs and testimony, please see **[[Participation|participation]]**. Preserving these names is part of preserving what was done to them.

![Joshua Wong Chi-fung, 2017](/assets/joshua-wong.jpg)
*Joshua Wong Chi-fung in 2017. Photo: Voice of America, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Joshua_Wong_Chi-fung,_2017_(cropped).jpg).*

**Joshua Wong Chi-fung** (黃之鋒, born 13 October 1996) is the best-known figure of Hong Kong's youth protest movement — the schoolboy activist who became the global face of the **2014 Umbrella Movement** and, a decade later, one of the most heavily prosecuted people under the National Security Law. He has been **in custody since 2020**, is serving a sentence in the [[Hong Kong 47|hong-kong-47]] subversion case, and in **September 2026 pleaded guilty to a second national-security charge** that carries a maximum of **life imprisonment**.

## The student who took on Beijing

Wong first came to prominence at **15**. In 2011 he co-founded the student group **Scholarism** (學民思潮); in 2012 he led the campaign against a compulsory "moral and national education" curriculum critics saw as pro-Beijing indoctrination, drawing a rally of some **100,000 people** and forcing the government to shelve the plan.

Two years later he was a leading face of the **2014 Umbrella Movement**, the 79-day occupation demanding genuine universal suffrage. His arrest during the storming of Civic Square helped trigger the sit-ins. The image of a bespectacled teenager facing down Beijing made him internationally famous — named to *Time*'s "25 Most Influential Teens," later the subject of the Netflix documentary *Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower* (2017), and in **2018 nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize** alongside fellow Umbrella leaders.

## Demosistō and disqualification

In 2016 Wong co-founded the pro-democracy party **Demosistō** (香港眾志) with **Nathan Law** and **Agnes Chow**, campaigning for Hong Kong's right to self-determination. He was repeatedly barred from running for or holding office. On **30 June 2020**, hours before the National Security Law took effect, Wong, Law and Chow quit the party and Demosistō disbanded — its parting message: "We will meet again."

## A decade in and out of prison

Even before the NSL, Wong was jailed again and again over the protests he led — for the 2014 storming of **Civic Square**, for contempt over the Mong Kok occupation, for organising the June 2019 siege of **police headquarters** during the anti-extradition-bill movement, and for attending banned **June 4th vigils**. He has been continuously imprisoned since December 2020.

## The Hong Kong 47

Wong was among the [[Hong Kong 47|hong-kong-47]] — the democrats prosecuted for organising the 2020 opposition **primary election**. He **pleaded guilty** to conspiracy to commit subversion and, in **November 2024**, was sentenced to **4 years 8 months**. He had been due for release in **2027**.

## A second case — up to life

On **6 June 2025**, while already in prison, Wong was hit with a **fresh charge**: conspiracy to **collude with foreign forces**. Prosecutors say that in 2020 he lobbied foreign governments — chiefly the United States — to **impose sanctions or a blockade** on Hong Kong and China, and kept up that campaign after the NSL made it a crime.

On **2 September 2026** Wong **pleaded guilty** to the charge at the High Court. The offence carries **three to ten years**, rising to **up to life imprisonment** if the court finds it "of a grave nature" — meaning the 29-year-old, rather than walking free in 2027, could face many more years behind bars ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2026/09/02/breaking-jailed-hong-kong-pro-democracy-campaigner-joshua-wong-pleads-guilty-to-foreign-collusion-charge/) · [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/2/hong-kong-activist-joshua-wong-pleads-guilty-in-national-security-case) · [RFA](https://www.rfa.org/english/china/2026/09/02/joshua-wong-guilty-plea-hong-kong-national-security-law/)). Sentencing is expected later.

## Even the film is under review (2026)

Wong's story reached a global audience through **_Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower_** (2017), the 78-minute Netflix documentary by American director **Joe Piscatella** that follows his Scholarism years and features **Nathan Law** and **Agnes Chow**. Nearly a decade on, the film itself became a target. On **15 September 2026**, Hong Kong's **Security Bureau** said it was "**taking follow-up action**" over the documentary — still streamable in the city, rated 13+ — stressing that "**all films broadcast in the city must meet Hong Kong law**," including the National Security Law and the 2024 Safeguarding National Security Ordinance. Whether any act amounts to a crime, it said, "depends on the facts and circumstances of each case" and "cannot be judged in the abstract"; if violations were found, "law-enforcement agencies will act according to the law" ([Dim Sum Daily](https://www.dimsumdaily.hk/security-bureau-reviewing-netflix-film-on-joshua-wong/)).

Back in 2020, as the NSL took effect, Netflix had signalled it would not "**proactively**" pull the film and would act only on a formal government takedown request ([HKFP](https://hongkongfp.com/2020/07/10/security-law-netflix-will-not-proactively-remove-joshua-wong-documentary-source/)). The review extends the city's censorship drive — already felt by its [[bookshops|book-censorship]] and the [[Tiananmen vigil|tiananmen-vigil]] — to an international streaming platform, and raised the prospect that merely hosting a film about a jailed activist could be cast as a security offence. The film sits within the archive's wider record of [[Hong Kong protest films|films]].

## Recognition

Wong's activism made him one of the movement's most decorated figures abroad — *Time*'s most-influential-teens list (2014), *Fortune*'s "World's Greatest Leaders" (2015), a **2018 Nobel Peace Prize nomination**, and the co-author of *Unfree Speech: The Threat to Global Democracy and Why We Must Act, Now* (2020), with a foreword by last colonial governor **Chris Patten** and an introduction by artist **Ai Weiwei**. To Beijing he became a symbol of "foreign-backed" subversion; to his supporters, of a generation jailed for asking to choose its own government.

Jimmy Lai Chee-ying (黎智英, born 8 December 1947) is a Hong Kong media entrepreneur and pro-democracy activist. He founded Giordano clothing, Next Digital media group, and Apple Daily newspaper. A naturalized British citizen, Lai became one of the most prominent voices supporting Hong Kong's democracy movement.

## Case & Sentencing

- **2020-08-10** Lai arrested under the National Security Law along with his sons and several Apple Daily executives
- **2020-12** Charged with foreign collusion under the NSL
- **2021-06-23** Apple Daily forced to close after asset freezes and executive arrests
- **2021-12** Trial begins at West Kowloon Courts
- **2024-12-19** Convicted of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces and sedition
- **2026-02-09** Sentenced to 20 years imprisonment; six co-defendants receive 6 years 9 months to 10 years
- **2026-02-26** Court of Appeal **quashes his separate 2022 fraud conviction** (illegal subletting of Apple Daily office space at a government-owned media park to Dico Consultants); codefendant Wong Wai-keung also cleared and the ~6-year sentence set aside, the judges ruling the lease breach did not reach the criminal threshold for fraud — a rare legal win that reduces his total prison time
- **2026-03-05** Legal team confirms Lai **will not appeal** the national-security conviction or 20-year sentence, citing "clear and definitive instructions"; analysts suggest non-appeal may be a precondition for any diplomatic/humanitarian deal, though it guarantees nothing
